📚 Reference Links

  • The SSE wire format and flush semantics (normative) — WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events

  • proxy_buffering, proxy_read_timeout, X-Accel-Buffering — nginx ngx_http_proxy_module

  • What a provider stream actually emits — Claude Docs: Streaming messages

  • Chunked transfer and response framing — RFC 9112 §7.1: Chunked Transfer Coding

  • Bonus — MDN: Using server-sent events

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
How many places can buffer a token stream? Five: app framework, compression, reverse proxy, load balancer, CDN. All default to buffering or compressing.
The nginx pair that fixes it? proxy_buffering off; and gzip off; — or X-Accel-Buffering: no per response.
Why does gzip break streaming even with buffering off? The compressor fills its window before emitting; it batches your tokens invisibly.
What does buffering do to your metrics? Nothing. Same status, same duration, same bytes. Only TTFT moves.
How do you prove it end-to-end? curl -N from outside the edge. If it dribbles it works; if it dumps, something buffers.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Token streaming is SSE over ordinary HTTP, and the protocol is the easy part. The hard part is that every hop between the model and the browser buffers by default — your web framework's response buffer, gzip's compression window, nginx's proxy_buffering, the load balancer, and the CDN. Any one of them turns token-by-token delivery into a single dump at the end. Total latency, status code and byte count are all identical, so nothing on a normal dashboard shows it. The only signal is time-to-first-token, and the only proof is curl -N from outside the edge.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through every hop that can buffer, and what turns it off.

Start at the application. Most frameworks buffer the response body and flush on completion, so a generator or async iterator has to be paired with an explicit flush per chunk — in ASGI that's yielding from a streaming response and not wrapping it in anything that collects; in a servlet stack it's calling flush() on the writer after each write. If your app doesn't flush, nothing downstream can help.

Then compression. gzip and brotli fill a window before emitting output, which batches tokens even when every other setting is correct. This is the one people miss because it isn't called buffering. Either disable compression on the streaming route or configure the compressor to flush per chunk — and note that a token is tens of bytes, so compression buys you almost nothing here anyway.

Then the reverse proxy. nginx's proxy_buffering defaults to on, which accumulates the upstream response into buffers and forwards when they fill or the response ends — i.e. never, for a stream. proxy_buffering off in the location, or X-Accel-Buffering: no from the origin, fixes it; the header is safer because it's per-response rather than per-route.

Then the load balancer and the CDN. Cloud L7 balancers generally stream, but their idle timeouts cut you. The CDN is the most dangerous hop, because buffering is often the point of the product and the fix is a bypass rule someone can undo in a console without touching your code.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Should the streaming path go through your CDN at all?

Routing it through the CDN keeps one hostname, one TLS termination point, one WAF and one set of edge rules, which is worth real money in operational simplicity — and a CDN's warm TLS session to the origin genuinely shaves connection setup for the first request. The risk is that the CDN's default behaviour is to buffer and cache, so your token stream depends on a configuration living outside your repository, changed by people who don't know it's load-bearing.

Bypassing the CDN for the streaming route removes that failure mode and costs you a second hostname, a second certificate, a second place to configure WAF rules and rate limits, and a slightly colder connection path. It also fragments your edge logging, which matters more than teams expect during an incident.

I'd keep the streaming path on the CDN and defend it with a test rather than a policy: a synthetic check from outside the edge that asserts inter-token gaps, running continuously. That converts "someone might change the config" from an invisible risk into a failing alarm, which is the only durable answer when the control plane isn't yours.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At 10,000 concurrent streams through one gateway tier, what runs out?

Not CPU. Each stream is an open connection with kernel send and receive buffers plus whatever your framework allocates per request, so the first ceiling is file descriptors and memory — tens of KB per connection means 10,000 streams is a memory conversation before it's a compute one, and ulimit -n plus somaxconn are the settings that bite first.

The second is HTTP/2 flow control, which is easy to miss because it's per stream. Each stream starts with a 65,535-octet window, and a client that reads slowly stops sending WINDOW_UPDATE, so your gateway's write blocks. If the gateway then queues tokens in userspace instead of propagating that stall to the model server, one slow reader becomes unbounded memory — the classic slow-consumer failure, arriving here with GPU-generated data behind it.

Third is the gateway's concurrency model: a thread-per-request server with 10,000 open streams needs 10,000 threads, which is why streaming gateways run on async runtimes and why "add streaming to the existing service" is sometimes a rewrite.

How it presents matters — existing streams keep flowing perfectly while new connections hang in the accept queue, and request-rate dashboards look normal because there is nothing new to count. The signal is client-side connect-error rate, which nobody graphs by default.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the streaming path for a chat product across web, mobile and a partner API.

🎯 Really testing: whether you make the generation independent of the connection.

The highest-stakes constraint is that a generation costs GPU-seconds and a dropped connection must not mean a re-run. So the generation is a resource with an id, not a property of the socket: POST the prompt, get a generation id, then GET /generations/{id}/stream. Tokens are appended to a short-lived per-generation buffer as they're produced, so a reconnect with Last-Event-ID replays the gap and continues live. That one decision also gives the partner API a 202-plus-poll option and the mobile client a resume-on-foreground path, from the same state.

The hops are client → CDN (streaming route with buffering and compression disabled) → L7 LB (idle timeout above the longest expected quiet gap) → inference gateway (async runtime, holds connections, propagates backpressure) → model servers. The gateway is the only tier that knows connections exist; everything upstream of it deals in generation ids.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is time-to-first-token split by hop, plus the p99 inter-token gap. TTFT catches a cold path or a queue in front of the model; the inter-token gap catches partial buffering that TTFT alone misses — a proxy that flushes headers immediately and then batches the body looks perfect on TTFT and terrible to a user.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Hop Default behaviour What it looks like when wrong The fix
App framework buffers, flushes at end nothing streams at all, even locally explicit flush per chunk; a true streaming response type
Compression (gzip/brotli) fills a window before emitting tokens arrive in bursts of 10–50 gzip off on the route, or per-chunk flush mode
nginx / reverse proxy proxy_buffering on works locally, dumps at the end in prod proxy_buffering off or X-Accel-Buffering: no
L7 load balancer streams, but times out idle stream dies mid-generation after 60s raise idle timeout; heartbeat comments
CDN buffers and caches same as nginx, but configured outside your repo streaming/bypass rule + a synthetic gap check
Client SDK may buffer its own reads app sees complete text only use the streaming API, not the convenience wrapper

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Five people relaying a sentence, and every one of them wants to wait for the full stop.

📖 Story

You dictate a sentence word by word down a line of five relayers. Each one, left alone, waits politely until you finish before passing anything on — so the listener at the end hears nothing, then hears everything at once. You have to tell each of them separately, in their own language, "say it as you hear it." Tell four and forget the fifth, and the listener still hears silence then a burst.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • five relayers = app framework, compressor, reverse proxy, load balancer, CDN

  • "waits for the full stop" = buffering until the response completes

  • "in their own language" = a different setting at each hop: flush(), gzip off, proxy_buffering off, an edge rule

  • "forget the fifth" = the one misconfigured hop that makes the other four irrelevant — buffering is not partially fixable

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

What "flush" actually means at each layer

A flush is a write that reaches the socket rather than an internal buffer, and every layer has its own idea of when that happens. In the application it's an explicit call or a genuinely lazy iterator. In the compressor it's a sync-flush that emits a deflate block boundary — which costs a few bytes per flush and is why per-chunk compression of tiny payloads is pointless. In nginx it's the difference between proxy_buffering on, which reads upstream as fast as possible into buffers, and off, which forwards synchronously as data arrives. In HTTP/1.1 the wire encoding is chunked transfer coding: each chunk is a hex length, CRLF, the bytes, CRLF. On HTTP/2 there's no chunked encoding — the stream is DATA frames — but the same flush question applies one layer up.

The math: TTFT versus total latency

For a 40-token response at 28 ms per token, total generation is about 1.1 seconds. With a healthy path, the user sees text at ~355 ms and reads along as it arrives. With one buffering hop, the user sees nothing for ~1.5 seconds and then everything. Total latency is identical. The perceived difference is the full 1.1 seconds of streaming, which is why this is a product bug that no latency dashboard reports.

The general form: perceived latency is TTFT when streaming works and TTFT + n·t_token when it doesn't, so the damage grows linearly with response length. A 500-token answer at 28 ms is 14 seconds of staring at a spinner — which is why long-form outputs are where users notice first and file the bug.

Backpressure, in one paragraph

HTTP/2's per-stream window (65,535 octets initially) is what stops a fast generator overwhelming a slow reader, and it's the good case: the stall propagates to the gateway, which should propagate it to the model server or stop reading. The bad case is a gateway that buffers tokens in userspace ahead of the socket, absorbing the signal — memory then grows per slow client with no error anywhere. Bound the per-connection outbound queue and choose a policy: disconnect and let the client resume by Last-Event-ID, which is the right answer when the buffer exists anyway.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is time-to-first-token, and the reason it matters is that users judge a streaming product entirely on it. A buffered stream has identical total latency, identical status codes, identical byte counts and identical error rates — the whole degradation is invisible to standard monitoring and completely obvious to every user. That asymmetry is why this note exists: it is the highest-frequency, lowest-visibility failure in AI product infrastructure.

The second reason is cost. When the connection dies mid-generation — an idle timeout, a mobile NAT eviction, a deploy — the model usually keeps generating, because a dropped TCP flow produces no FIN and the server learns about it seconds or minutes later. Every one of those is GPU time billed for output nobody received. Making the generation an addressable resource with a replay buffer converts that from waste into a resumable stream, which is a cost argument as much as a UX one.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

location /v1/stream {
    proxy_pass http://inference_gateway;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;           # 1.0 disables chunked upstream keepalive
    proxy_set_header Connection "";   # strip hop-by-hop close so the upstream conn is reused
    proxy_buffering off;              # THE line — default is `on`, which holds the whole stream
    gzip off;                         # the compressor batches tokens even with buffering off
    proxy_cache off;                  # a cached token stream is a permanently wrong one
    chunked_transfer_encoding on;
    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;         # default 60s: a long quiet gap kills the generation
    proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
}

# ASGI: a genuinely lazy generator. Returning a list here would buffer the whole response.
@app.post("/v1/stream")
async def stream(req: Request):
    async def gen():
        async for tok in model.generate(req.prompt):
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'text': tok})}\n\n"   # blank line dispatches the event
            # no explicit flush needed in ASGI — but never wrap this in anything that collects
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"X-Accel-Buffering": "no", "Cache-Control": "no-cache"})

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Scenario: the config above, a 40-token completion, traced with curl -N from outside the CDN — and the same request with one hop misconfigured.

📥 [0ms]   GET /v1/stream   Accept: text/event-stream
    │
    ▼
📡 [1] CDN: streaming rule matched → no cache, no buffer, headers forwarded
    │
    ▼
⚖️ [2] ALB → gateway. Headers reach the client at ~40ms (TTFB)
    │
    ▼
🤖 [3] model server: 210ms queue wait, first token at 340ms
    │
    ▼
🎯 [4] "data: {\"text\":\"An\"}" flushed at 355ms  → TTFT = 355ms ✅
    │
    ▼
📊 [5] tokens 2..40 at ~28ms apart; p99 inter-token gap 34ms; done at 1.47s
    │
════ same request, gzip left ON at nginx ════
    ▼
⚠️ [6] TTFB still 40ms (headers are not compressed) — dashboards unchanged
    │
    ▼
❌ [7] first visible token at 1.42s; all 40 arrive within 60ms of each other
       TTFT 1.42s, total 1.48s. Status 200. Bytes identical. Nothing alerts.

1. TTFB and TTFT are different numbers and only one is interesting. Headers came back in 40 ms in both runs. The gap between 355 ms and 1.42 s is the entire user experience, and no metric derived from request duration can see it. Instrument the first body byte at the client, not the first response byte.

2. Step 3's 210 ms of queue wait is not a network problem. Splitting TTFT into queue time, model prefill and network time is what stops "streaming is slow" turning into a fruitless proxy investigation. If queue time dominates, the answer is capacity or routing, not buffering.

3. Step 6 is why gzip is the sneakiest hop. Compression doesn't touch headers, so TTFB is unaffected and every proxy-level check passes. The compressor is holding token bytes in a window that only flushes when it fills — which for 30-byte SSE records takes dozens of tokens.

4. The p99 inter-token gap in step 5 is the metric that catches partial buffering. A hop that flushes headers and then batches the body gives you a perfect TTFT and a terrible experience. Gap p99 is the only number that distinguishes them, and it belongs on the same dashboard.

5. curl -N is the diagnostic, and the -N matters. Without it, curl buffers its own output and you will blame the server for your terminal. Run it from outside the CDN, not from inside the VPC, or you skip the hop most likely to be wrong.

10. When TO Use This

  • Any user-facing generation — chat, completion, summarisation, code assistance. If a human is waiting for text, streaming is the difference between a product that feels alive and one that feels broken.

  • Long-form output especially — the perceived-latency penalty of a buffered stream grows linearly with response length, so the longer your typical answer, the more this matters.

  • Progressive tool-use and agent traces — streaming intermediate steps ("searching…", "reading document 3") is often more valuable than streaming tokens, because it explains a long wait rather than hiding it.

  • Any path where a partner or customer integrates with your streaming API — they will hit exactly these hops on their side too, and your docs should say which headers you send.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not when the output is atomic. A JSON object the client can't use until it's complete — a structured extraction, a classification — gains nothing from streaming and costs you a held connection. Return it whole.

  • Not for batch work. Minutes-to-hours jobs belong behind 202 and a job resource; a streaming connection held for an hour is a bet against every idle timeout on the path.

  • Not without a resume story on expensive generations. Streaming into a connection with no per-generation buffer means every dropped connection is wasted GPU time and a user who has to re-ask.

  • Not through infrastructure you can't test. If you can't run a synthetic inter-token-gap check through the real edge, you don't know whether streaming works — you know it worked the last time someone looked.

  • Not with compression enabled to "save bandwidth". SSE token records are tens of bytes; compression saves a rounding error and costs you the entire streaming behaviour.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Streaming works — I tested it locally."

✅ Reality: Your dev server has no reverse proxy, no CDN and usually no compression. The five hops that break streaming are exactly the ones absent from localhost. The only valid test is curl -N through the production edge.

❌ Misconception: "If buffering were happening, latency would go up."

✅ Reality: Total latency is unchanged — the same bytes arrive at the same final moment. What changes is when the first byte arrives, and nothing in a standard request-duration metric captures that. This is why the bug survives for months in products that monitor everything else.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought proxy_buffering off was the fix, singular. It's one of five, and gzip is the one that survives it — headers flush, TTFB looks perfect, and tokens still arrive in bursts because the compressor is filling its window. Buffering is not partially fixable: four correct hops and one wrong one gives you exactly the same user experience as zero correct hops.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing SSE and stopping at the protocol. The wire format is trivial and nobody is testing it. The discussion is the path — which hops buffer, which setting fixes each, and how you'd prove it. Get there in the first thirty seconds.

Naming one hop. "We turn off proxy buffering" is a partial answer that invites the follow-up you'll fail. Enumerate: app flush, compression, proxy, LB timeout, CDN.

Confusing TTFB with TTFT. They diverge by exactly the amount that matters on a streaming endpoint, and naming them separately is a fast signal you've operated one.

Ignoring the write side. People describe tokens flowing outward and never mention what happens when the client reads slowly or vanishes. Backpressure and cancellation-that-doesn't-arrive are half of this topic in production.

No answer for a dropped connection. Every long generation will lose some connections. If there's no per-generation buffer and no Last-Event-ID replay, the honest answer is "we re-run it", and that's a cost line you should name rather than skip.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
nginx proxy_buffering default on The canonical cause of "works locally, broken in prod" nginx docs
nginx proxy_read_timeout default 60s Between successive reads — a long prefill or quiet gap dies nginx docs
AWS ALB idle timeout default 60s Applies to the whole streaming connection AWS ELB docs

SSE record overhead ~8 bytes + optional id:/event: Why compressing a token stream buys almost nothing WHATWG HTML §9.2

Chunked framing hex length + CRLF per chunk HTTP/1.1 only; HTTP/2 uses DATA frames RFC 9112 §7.1

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Streaming doesn't reduce total latency at all — it moves the user's first signal from the end to ~350ms, which is the entire benefit
💰 Cost Disabling compression on the streaming route costs bandwidth measured in kilobytes; a dropped connection mid-generation costs GPU-seconds
🔒 Security / visibility Staying on plain HTTP keeps WAF, auth and per-tenant limits working; a bypassed edge hostname fragments all three
📈 Scale Concurrency is connections, not requests — sized by file descriptors and memory, and an event-loop runtime is close to mandatory
🔧 Ops complexity The critical config lives in five places, at least one of which (the CDN) is outside your repository and outside code review
🐛 Debuggability Excellent with curl -N, which shows the exact bytes and their timing — the single best debugging property of this stack

16. Real World Usage

Provider inference APIs all stream over HTTP+SSE with stream: true, emitting typed events for message start, content deltas and completion. Standardising on that shape is why every gateway, proxy and SDK in the ecosystem speaks the same wire format — and why the buffering problem is universal rather than product-specific.

Coding assistants and agent UIs stream tool-use steps as well as tokens: a thirty-second wait explained ("running tests…") is tolerable and the same wait unexplained is not, which makes the streaming path load-bearing even when the final answer is short.

Any product with a CDN in front of its API eventually files this bug at least once, typically after an edge configuration change nobody associated with the AI feature. It is the strongest argument for a continuous synthetic gap check rather than a one-time verification.

17. Acronym Decoder

TTFT — Time To First Token: the interval from request to the first visible token. Distinct from TTFB (Time To First Byte), which is when response headers arrive — the two are equal on a normal API and diverge by the entire generation time when a hop buffers, which is exactly why both names exist.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

"Design the serving path for a chat assistant" lands here immediately, and the probe is whether you talk about the path rather than the protocol. The strong answer names the five buffering hops unprompted, makes the generation addressable so a reconnect resumes instead of re-running, splits TTFT into queue and network components, and proposes a synthetic check rather than trusting configuration. It's also the section where the cost argument — GPU time spent on abandoned generations — separates people who've run this from people who've built a demo.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
1k concurrent streams Gateway fds and per-connection memory Async runtime, raised ulimit -n, minimal per-stream state
10k concurrent streams Per-generation buffers in the replay store; h2 flow-control stalls from slow readers Cap buffer length and TTL; bound the outbound queue and disconnect-with-resume
100k concurrent streams Deploy-time reconnect storms; single-region gateway tier Server-set jittered retry:, connection draining, regional gateway tiers

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, the replay buffer is the memory ceiling before connection count is, because every in-flight generation holds its tokens twice.

  • At 100x, a rolling deploy severs every stream at once and identical reconnect delays turn it into a synchronised wave at the edge.

  • Operationally, the 3am version is a CDN configuration change that re-enables buffering: no errors, no latency change, and every user reporting the product "stopped streaming".

Monitoring & SLOs

  • TTFT p50/p99, split into queue time, model prefill and network — the SLI users feel, and the split is what makes it actionable.

  • Inter-token gap p99 — catches partial buffering that TTFT alone misses.

  • Abandoned-generation rate and GPU-seconds spent on them — the cost metric that justifies the replay buffer.

  • Synthetic streaming check through the real edge — asserts inter-token gaps continuously, so an edge config change fails an alarm rather than a user.

📚 Reference Links

  • TLS 1.3 handshake, 1-RTT and 0-RTT resumption (normative) — RFC 8446 §2

  • Connection reuse, TLS cost and the protocol arc — hpbn.co: Transport Layer Security (TLS)

  • Multiplexing, so the stream doesn't wait on a new connection — RFC 9113: HTTP/2

  • Where the prefill time goes on the model side — vLLM: Automatic Prefix Caching

  • Bonus — Claude Docs: Streaming messages

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
RTTs before the first request byte, cold connection, TLS 1.3? 1 for TCP + 1 for TLS = 2. TLS 1.2 was 3. Session resumption or 0-RTT removes the TLS one.
The single biggest network saving available? Connection reuse — a warm keep-alive connection costs zero setup RTTs.
Which part of TTFT is usually the largest? Queue wait plus prefill at the model server, not the network — measure before optimising.
What does prefill cost scale with? Prompt length. Long system prompts and big RAG contexts are a TTFT tax on every request.
The one number that makes TTFT actionable? Its split: setup + edge + gateway + queue + prefill. An unsplit TTFT tells you nothing.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Time-to-first-token is a budget with five line items: connection setup, edge-to-origin transit, gateway hops, queue wait at the model server, and prefill compute. On a cold connection the network half is two round trips — one TCP, one TLS 1.3 — which is 50 to 250 milliseconds depending on distance, and connection reuse removes all of it. But on a warm path the network is usually the small half; queue wait and prefill dominate. So the first move is always to split the number, because optimising proxies when the answer is a 200-millisecond queue is a wasted quarter.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Break TTFT down. Where does the time actually go?

Five components, in order of when they happen. Connection setup: DNS if uncached, then one RTT for the TCP handshake and one for TLS 1.3 — TLS 1.2 needed two. On a warm keep-alive connection all of this is zero, which is why it's the first thing to check rather than the first thing to optimise. Edge to origin: if you terminate TLS at a CDN edge near the user, the user's handshake RTTs are short and the long haul happens on a pre-warmed origin connection, so distance stops multiplying.

Gateway hops: every proxy, auth check, rate limiter and mesh sidecar adds a small amount, and they add up in a way nobody budgets for — five hops at 3 ms each is 15 ms of pure overhead before your service sees the request. Queue wait: how long the request sits before the model server starts it, which is a function of load, batching policy and routing. Prefill: computing the KV cache for the prompt, which scales with prompt length and is where a 4,000-token system prompt quietly costs you every single request.

Enumerate them because the fixes are entirely different: connection reuse and TLS resumption for setup, removing hops for the gateway, capacity or routing for the queue, and shorter prompts or cached prefixes for prefill — a serving decision, not a network one.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Terminate TLS at the edge, or pass through to origin?

Edge termination is the default for a reason. The user's two setup round trips happen against a point of presence tens of milliseconds away rather than a region that might be 200 milliseconds away, and the edge holds a warm, multiplexed connection to your origin, so the long haul costs no handshake at all. On a cold client connection from a distant user that's often the single largest saving available — hundreds of milliseconds, for a configuration change.

The cost is that the edge sees plaintext — fine for most products, disqualifying if compliance requires end-to-end encryption to your own infrastructure or the prompts carry regulated data. Then pass-through is the answer and you accept the RTTs. The middle ground is edge termination with a re-encrypted origin leg.

I'd terminate at the edge for a consumer product and re-encrypt to origin, then spend the saved effort on prompt length and routing, because those usually dominate on a warm path. What I wouldn't do is argue about it before measuring the split — if 70% of your TTFT is queue wait, the TLS decision is a rounding error.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Your p99 TTFT is four times your p50. What's causing it, and what runs out?

📍 Seen in the wild: the tail-latency probe on any serving design.

The usual cause is queueing, and queueing behaves non-linearly. As utilisation climbs past roughly 70–80%, waiting time rises sharply for the same arrival rate — so a fleet that looks comfortably loaded on average has a tail dominated by requests that arrived during a burst. The second cause is prompt-length variance: prefill scales with tokens, so a mix of 200-token and 8,000-token prompts produces a bimodal TTFT distribution that a single percentile hides badly. The third is cold starts — a scaled-out replica loading weights, or a connection pool that had to open a fresh TLS connection because the pool was exhausted.

What runs out depends on the cause. Under queueing it's GPU capacity, and the symptom is queue-wait p99 rising while prefill stays flat. Under prompt variance nothing runs out — the fleet is fine and the metric is lying, which is why TTFT must be bucketed by prompt-length band. Under cold starts it's pool slots or replica warm-up, and the tell is that p99 correlates with scaling events rather than traffic.

Two cheap mitigations: separate long-prompt traffic onto its own pool so one class can't starve the other, and hedge — issue a second request to another replica if the first hasn't produced a token by the p95 — trading a few percent of load for a much tighter tail.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You have a 500 ms TTFT target for users on three continents. Design for it.

🎯 Really testing: whether you allocate a budget across hops rather than optimising one.

The highest-stakes constraint is the speed of light: a round trip between continents is 150–250 ms, and no engineering removes it. So the budget has to be written down first and allocated — say 60 ms for user-to-edge setup on a warm connection, 40 ms of gateway and auth, 120 ms of queue, 200 ms of prefill, leaving 80 ms of margin. Writing that down is what makes the design decisions obvious.

That budget forces two structural choices. Inference capacity in each region, because a transcontinental RTT alone eats half the budget and an edge CDN accelerates setup, not computation happening across an ocean. And connection reuse everywhere: warm edge-to-origin pools, HTTP/2 multiplexing so a new stream costs no handshake, TLS session resumption for reconnecting clients.

Prefill rewards the most attention and is the least network-shaped: a shared system prompt identical across requests can be served from a cached prefix, turning a fixed per-request cost into near zero. It belongs in the network budget conversation because it's often the largest item you can actually remove.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is regional TTFT divergence — one region drifting while the others are fine, which means capacity or routing in that region rather than anything global. A single global TTFT percentile hides exactly that.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Lever Typical saving Cost When it's the right move
Connection reuse (keep-alive, h2) 1–2 RTTs, 50–250 ms none — it's configuration Always. Check this before anything else
TLS 1.3 + session resumption 1 RTT on reconnect 0-RTT adds replay risk Clients that reconnect often; skip 0-RTT for non-idempotent requests
Edge TLS termination 1–2 long-haul RTTs edge sees plaintext Consumer products without end-to-end encryption requirements
Removing a gateway hop 2–10 ms each you lose whatever it did When you have five hops and can't say what two of them do
Regional inference capacity 150–250 ms cross-continent multi-region GPU cost Multi-continent products with a sub-second target
Prefix caching / shorter prompts often 100s of ms prompt-design discipline Large shared system prompts or RAG contexts — usually the biggest single win
Hedged requests tightens p99 a few % extra load Read-only generation where a duplicate is harmless

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Five queues at the airport, and you keep upgrading the shortest one.

📖 Story

You time your journey from door to gate: taxi, check-in, security, the walk, the queue at the desk. You buy a faster taxi and save four minutes, then discover security took forty. Nobody can tell you which line was the slow one unless someone timed each leg separately — so the first job is a stopwatch at every door, not a faster taxi.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • the five legs = connection setup, edge transit, gateway hops, queue wait, prefill

  • the faster taxi = optimising TLS or proxies before measuring

  • "security took forty" = queue wait at the model server, usually the dominant term

  • the stopwatch at every door = TTFT instrumented as a split, not a single number

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The budget, as arithmetic

TTFT is a sum, and writing it as one is what makes it manageable:

TTFT = setup + transit + gateway + queue + prefill

Only the first three are network terms, and on a warm connection the first is zero. The useful discipline is to allocate a target across the five and hold each one to its slice, rather than chasing whichever is loudest. A 500 ms target might be allocated 60 / 40 / 40 / 120 / 200 with 40 ms of margin — and the moment you write that down, "we need regional inference" stops being an opinion and becomes arithmetic, because a 200 ms transcontinental transit does not fit in a 40 ms slot.

The physics you cannot optimise

Light in fibre travels at roughly two-thirds of c, about 200,000 km/s, so a round trip is about 1 ms per 100 km of fibre — and real paths are longer than great-circle distance. That puts a hard floor under cross-continent latency: Mumbai to Virginia is on the order of 180–220 ms round trip, and no protocol change alters it. This is the number that turns "put a CDN in front of it" into "put inference capacity in the region", because a CDN accelerates setup, not computation that must happen on the other side of the ocean.

Where the handshakes go

A cold HTTPS request costs one RTT for TCP and one for TLS 1.3 — two before the request bytes leave. TLS 1.2 needed two for TLS, so three total; 0-RTT resumption removes the TLS round trip entirely at the cost of replay exposure, which makes it acceptable for idempotent requests and a bad idea for anything that mutates state. A warm connection costs none of this, which is why connection reuse is worth more than every other network lever combined and is also the one most often broken by accident — a pool sized too small, a proxy that closes connections, or Connection: close left in a header.

Tail behaviour

Queue wait doesn't grow linearly with load. Past roughly 70–80% utilisation, waiting time climbs steeply for the same arrival rate, which is why a fleet at "80% average" has a p99 several times its p50. And with prompt-length variance, TTFT is a mixture of distributions rather than one — so bucket the metric by prompt-length band before drawing conclusions, or you'll chase a tail that's really two populations.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is TTFT, and it is the metric users equate with product quality. Total generation time barely registers once text is moving; the wait before the first character is the entire perception of speed. Products that halve TTFT are described as "much faster" even when total latency is unchanged, which makes it one of the few infrastructure numbers with a direct, legible product effect.

The second reason is that TTFT is where network and serving engineering meet, usually badly instrumented. Network teams optimise handshakes that were already zero; serving teams optimise batching while a gateway adds five hops; nobody has the split. Producing it is the highest-leverage move available, and it costs a day of instrumentation rather than a quarter of optimisation.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Split the network half of TTFT with curl's timing variables — cold vs warm.
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '
 dns:      %{time_namelookup}s
 tcp:      %{time_connect}s
 tls:      %{time_appconnect}s
 ttfb:     %{time_starttransfer}s
 total:    %{time_total}s\n' \
  -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/messages \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d @prompt.json
# time_connect - time_namelookup  = the TCP RTT
# time_appconnect - time_connect  = the TLS handshake
# time_starttransfer - time_appconnect = server-side: gateway + queue + prefill
# Run it twice on one connection to see the warm number:
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{time_starttransfer}\n' --next -o /dev/null -w '%{time_starttransfer}\n' <url> <url>

upstream inference_gateway {
    server gw-1.internal:8443;
    keepalive 256;                 # THE setting — without it every proxied request
                                   # opens a new TCP+TLS connection to the upstream
    keepalive_timeout 300s;
    keepalive_requests 10000;      # default recycles connections early and re-pays handshakes
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Scenario: a user in Mumbai, edge PoP in Mumbai, inference in Mumbai; then the same request with inference in Virginia.

📥 [0ms]   POST /v1/messages, cold connection
    │
    ▼
🔒 [1] TCP handshake to PoP: 1 RTT = 24ms   (time_connect - time_namelookup)
    │
    ▼
🔒 [2] TLS 1.3: 1 RTT = 25ms                (time_appconnect - time_connect)
    │      ── 49ms of setup, and 0ms on the next request over the same connection
    ▼
📡 [3] edge → origin over a warm pooled h2 connection: 6ms, no handshake
    │
    ▼
🚦 [4] gateway: auth 3ms + rate limit 2ms + mesh sidecar 3ms = 8ms
    │
    ▼
⏱️ [5] scheduler queue: 118ms  ← the largest single term
    │
    ▼
🤖 [6] prefill, 2,400 prompt tokens: 176ms   (≈12ms with the shared prefix cached)
    │
    ▼
🎯 [7] first token → TTFT 357ms cold, 308ms warm ✅ (target 500ms)
    │
════ same request, model in Virginia ════
    ▼
❌ [8] steps 1–2 unchanged (edge is still local), but step 3 becomes 195ms
       TTFT ≈ 552ms warm. Over target, and no proxy tuning recovers it.

1. Steps 1–2 vanish on the second request, and that's the cheapest win available. Fifty milliseconds of setup on a cold connection is worth optimising only if your clients genuinely connect cold each time; for an app holding a connection, this is already zero and every hour spent on TLS tuning is misallocated.

2. Step 3 is the geography decision, and step 8 is the proof. A local edge fixes setup latency for a distant user and does nothing for transit to where the computation happens. Once the model is across an ocean, 195 ms is a physics bill — the only fix is capacity in region.

3. Step 4's 8 ms is small and worth naming anyway. Five hops at that scale is 40 ms — a tenth of the budget on plumbing. Ask of any gateway chain what each hop does and whether two could be one.

4. Step 5 is the largest term and it isn't a network problem. 118 ms of queue wait means the answer is capacity, routing, or admission control, and no amount of proxy or TLS work will touch it. This is precisely why an unsplit TTFT is dangerous: the number looks like latency, so it gets handed to whoever owns the network.

5. Step 6 is the biggest single lever in this trace. 176 ms of prefill for a 2,400-token prompt drops to roughly 12 ms when the shared system-prompt prefix is already cached. That's a serving feature, but it belongs in this budget conversation because it removes more milliseconds than every network change combined.

10. When TO Use This

  • Before any "our AI product feels slow" investigation — the split is the first deliverable, and it usually reassigns the problem to a different team than the one that was asked.

  • When setting a latency SLO — allocating a budget across the five terms turns a target into a set of design constraints, including whether multi-region inference is required.

  • When evaluating an architecture change — a new gateway, a mesh, an extra auth hop: each one has a millisecond price that should be checked against the budget rather than assumed negligible.

  • When prompt design changes — a longer system prompt or a bigger RAG context is a TTFT change on every request, and it should be reviewed as a latency decision, not just a quality one.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't optimise TTFT for batch work. A job that runs for twenty minutes doesn't care about 50 ms of handshake. That path wants 202 and a job resource, and TTFT is the wrong metric entirely.

  • Don't chase the network when the split says queue. The most common wasted quarter in this area is proxy and TLS tuning against a p99 that is 70% scheduler wait.

  • Don't enable TLS 0-RTT indiscriminately. It removes a round trip and accepts replay exposure; that's fine for idempotent reads and wrong for anything that mutates state or charges money.

  • Don't treat a single global TTFT percentile as the SLI. It hides regional divergence and prompt-length bimodality — two very different problems that both show up as "the tail got worse".

  • Don't add a CDN expecting it to fix cross-region compute. It accelerates connection setup and static assets. The generation still happens where the GPUs are.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "TTFT is a network metric, so the network team owns it."

✅ Reality: On a warm connection the network terms are often under a fifth of the total, with queue wait and prefill dominating. TTFT is a shared budget, and the first useful action is publishing the split so the right team gets the right slice.

❌ Misconception: "Putting a CDN in front of the API fixes latency for distant users."

✅ Reality: It fixes setup latency — the handshake RTTs happen against a nearby PoP. The request still has to reach the region where inference runs, and that transit is bounded by the speed of light. Sub-second targets across continents require capacity in region, not a better edge.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated prompt length as a quality and cost concern, not a latency one. Prefill scales with prompt tokens, so a 4,000-token system prompt is a fixed tax on the metric users feel most — and prefix caching removes most of it. It was the largest TTFT lever available and it wasn't on my network diagram at all.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Quoting TTFT without the split. A single number invites the wrong fix. Naming the five terms and saying which dominates is what makes the answer credible in one sentence.

Optimising handshakes that are already zero. If your clients hold connections, setup is not your problem. Ask about connection reuse before proposing TLS work.

Ignoring the speed of light. Claiming a sub-300 ms target across continents without regional capacity is a design that arithmetic rejects. State the RTT and let it settle the question.

Forgetting the hops you didn't build. Mesh sidecars, WAFs, auth services and rate limiters each add milliseconds. An answer that goes "client → model" has skipped the part that's actually configurable.

Reporting a global percentile. Regional divergence and prompt-length bimodality both hide inside one p99. Bucket by region and prompt band, or the metric will mislead you confidently.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Edge termination buys 1–2 long-haul RTTs; regional inference buys the transit itself and costs a second GPU footprint
💰 Cost Multi-region GPU capacity is the expensive lever; prefix caching and shorter prompts are nearly free and often larger
🔒 Security / visibility Edge TLS termination exposes plaintext at a third party; 0-RTT trades a round trip for replay exposure
📈 Scale Queue wait dominates the tail past ~70–80% utilisation, so headroom is a latency feature, not slack
🔧 Ops complexity Every hop you add for a good reason is a millisecond on the metric users feel; the budget makes that explicit
🐛 Debuggability curl -w gives you the network split for free; the server-side split needs deliberate instrumentation at the gateway

16. Real World Usage

Consumer chat products publish and defend TTFT as a headline metric, and the engineering that follows is mostly regional capacity plus prompt-prefix reuse rather than protocol work — which is a useful signal about where the milliseconds actually are.

Coding assistants are stricter still: a suggestion arriving after the developer typed the next character is worthless, which pushes toward smaller models placed closer rather than bigger models placed centrally.

Voice agents impose the hardest constraint, because TTFT sits inside a conversational turn budget where a few hundred milliseconds reads as an awkward pause — which is why that path uses a different transport and a much tighter budget.

17. Acronym Decoder

TTFT — Time To First Token: request start to the first token rendered. Distinct from TTFB (Time To First Byte, when headers arrive) and from prefill, the model-side computation of the prompt's KV cache — the three are routinely conflated, and separating them is most of what makes this metric actionable.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • 202 + polling — for batch work, where TTFT is not the metric at all

  • Smaller model placed closer — often beats a larger model placed centrally when the budget is tight

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Prefix caching and prompt design — usually the largest single lever in the budget

  • Connection pooling and HTTP/2 multiplexing — what keeps the setup terms at zero

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

"Design a chat product with a 500 ms first-token target for users in three regions" is the framing, and it's a budget question disguised as an architecture one. The probe is whether you allocate across hops before proposing anything, whether you know the speed-of-light floor well enough to reject a single-region design, and whether you identify prefill and queue wait as the dominant terms rather than reaching for TLS tuning. Publishing the split is the answer that separates measurement from guesswork.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
1 region, 100 rps Queue wait past ~75% GPU utilisation Headroom as a latency feature; admission control with 429 + Retry-After
3 regions, 1k rps Cross-region transit for misrouted users; per-region cold starts Latency-based DNS or anycast routing; warm replica floor per region
3 regions, 20k rps Prefill dominates; long-prompt traffic starves short-prompt traffic Prefix caching, separate pools by prompt-length band, hedging on the short pool

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, the p99 detaches from the p50 as utilisation crosses the queueing knee, and the fleet still looks "80% loaded".

  • At 100x, prompt-length variance turns TTFT into a bimodal distribution that a single percentile misreports in both directions.

  • Operationally, the 3am version is a connection-pool exhaustion between edge and origin: every request re-pays two setup RTTs, TTFT jumps by 50 ms globally, and nothing errors.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • TTFT p50/p99 split into setup, transit, gateway, queue and prefill — the SLI, and the split is what makes it assignable.

  • TTFT bucketed by region and by prompt-length band — the two dimensions that hide inside a global percentile.

  • Upstream connection reuse ratio — new connections per request should be near zero; a rise means a pool problem and a silent 50 ms tax.

  • Queue wait p99 versus GPU utilisation — plotted together, so the knee is visible before it becomes the tail.

📚 Reference Links

  • proxy_read_timeout and proxy_send_timeout — nginx ngx_http_proxy_module

  • Bonus — Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is the quiet gap that kills AI streams? Extended reasoning or a tool call — minutes of silence on an open connection.
How do you pick the heartbeat interval? Under half the smallest idle timeout on the path. Behind a 60s ALB, 20–25s.
The SSE heartbeat, concretely? A : comment line. Ignored by the client, resets every idle timer on the path.
What sizes a streaming gateway tier? Concurrent connections — file descriptors and memory — not CPU or request rate.
What's the guaranteed mass-disconnection event? Your own rolling deploy, mid-generation, at GPU cost.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An AI stream is a connection held open for minutes, and everything on the path is configured to kill idle connections in sixty seconds. Extended reasoning and tool calls produce long silences that look exactly like a hung connection, so you send heartbeat comments well inside the shortest timeout and raise the timeouts you control. The tier is sized by concurrent connections rather than request rate — file descriptors and memory, not CPU. And because a dropped connection means GPU time already spent, deploys need draining and generations need to be resumable rather than restarted.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Which timeouts are actually on the path, and how do you pick a heartbeat?

Enumerate every hop and take the minimum. A cloud L7 load balancer commonly defaults to 60 seconds of idle. nginx's proxy_read_timeout and proxy_send_timeout both default to 60 seconds and apply between successive reads, not to the whole response. A CDN has its own origin-response timeout. Carrier NAT evicts an idle TCP flow somewhere around 30–60 seconds. Corporate proxies vary and are usually the shortest thing on the path. Client SDKs have their own read timeouts, often 30 seconds by default.

The heartbeat then falls out: interval under half the minimum, so a single lost heartbeat doesn't cost the connection. Behind a 60-second ALB that's 20–25 seconds. In SSE the heartbeat is a comment line — a : followed by anything — which the client parser ignores and every intermediary treats as data on the connection. It costs a handful of bytes and it is the difference between a five-minute generation surviving and dying at sixty seconds with a 504 the user reads as a product failure.

The subtlety worth naming is that raising your own timeouts is necessary and not sufficient. You control the ALB and nginx; you do not control the user's carrier NAT or their employer's proxy. Heartbeats are what defend against the hops you can't configure.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

One long connection for a whole generation, or 202 plus a job resource?

Holding the connection gives the best experience when it works: tokens arrive as produced, no polling, no extra round trips, and the client's mental model is simple. It works well up to a few minutes on a path you control end to end, and it's the right default for interactive chat.

The job-resource shape decouples the generation from the connection: POST returns an id, the client streams or polls against that id, and a dropped connection resumes rather than restarts. It costs an extra round trip and a state store, and it buys three things — resumption without re-running the model, a path that survives clients you don't control, and the ability to serve the same work to a browser, a mobile app in the background, and a partner API from one resource.

My rule: the moment a generation can exceed the shortest timeout you can't configure, make it a resource. In practice that means anything with tool use, extended reasoning, or a long RAG pipeline — because those are exactly the cases where a mobile client on a carrier network will drop mid-generation, and where re-running is expensive. Interactive short-form chat can stay on a held connection with heartbeats, and even then the per-generation buffer is worth having so Last-Event-ID actually resumes something.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

50,000 concurrent streams, generations averaging 90 seconds. What runs out?

📍 Seen in the wild: the scaling probe on any inference-gateway design.

Not CPU. The gateway is mostly waiting, so what runs out is file descriptors and per-connection memory: a socket plus kernel send and receive buffers plus per-request framework state, commonly tens of KB, which makes 50,000 streams a ulimit -n and heap conversation. Behind that, somaxconn and the accept backlog decide what happens when a burst arrives. And the concurrency model decides whether this is possible at all — a thread-per-request server needs 50,000 threads, which is why streaming gateways run on async runtimes.

The second ceiling is the load balancer's own per-node connection budget, and it matters more here than in ordinary HTTP because connections pin for their whole life. Fleet capacity is nodes × per-node ceiling, adding nodes does nothing for connections already placed, and a drain severs everything it drains.

The third is the one specific to this domain: each live connection has GPU work behind it. A slow client that stops reading stalls the write path, and if the gateway buffers tokens in userspace instead of propagating that stall, memory grows per slow client while the model keeps generating. Bound the per-connection outbound queue and choose a policy — disconnect and let the client resume by sequence id is usually right, because the buffer that makes resumption possible already exists.

How it presents: existing streams keep flowing perfectly while new connections hang in the accept queue. Request-rate dashboards look normal because there are no new requests. The signal is client-side connect-error rate and fd utilisation, neither of which is on a default dashboard.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design a deploy for a 50,000-connection inference gateway where generations cost real money.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat a rollout as a designed traffic event with a cost dimension.

The highest-stakes constraint is that severing a connection mid-generation wastes GPU-seconds already spent and forces the user to re-ask, so the rollout's success criterion is completed generations, not restart time. That makes drain-with-grace the core mechanism: a node deregisters from the load balancer so it takes no new streams, then keeps serving its existing generations until they finish or a grace window expires.

The grace window is computed, not guessed: set it above the p99 generation duration so the overwhelming majority complete naturally. For a 90-second average with a p99 near 5 minutes, that's a 6-minute drain per node, and terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed it or the orchestrator kills the pod mid-drain. Whatever remains at the end gets a "going away" event carrying a jittered reconnect delay, and resumes on another node from the per-generation buffer using Last-Event-ID.

The jitter is arithmetic: connections dropped over a window W against a fleet accepting A per second needs W > C/A, so 5,000 stragglers against 2,000 accepts/second needs at least a few seconds of spread, and more if the remaining fleet is smaller. Without it the reconnect wave overruns the accept queues and the retry loop keeps everyone out — an outage you caused with a routine deploy.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is generations severed per rollout, with GPU-seconds wasted attached to it. That's the number that makes the drain window a business decision rather than an infrastructure preference, and it's the one that gets the grace period raised when someone tries to shorten it.

Corporate / carrier proxy varies, often shortest ❌ heartbeats — the only defence
Mobile carrier NAT ~30–60s of silence ❌ heartbeats
CDN origin response vendor-specific yes, per route raise on the streaming path
L7 load balancer 60s (ALB default) yes raise well above p99 generation
nginx proxy_read_timeout 60s yes raise on the streaming location
TCP keepalive (Linux) 7200s yes, but useless as a check never rely on it

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Say something every twenty seconds or the line goes dead.

📖 Story

You're on a call with someone who thinks for four minutes before answering. Six different switchboards between you each assume a silent line is a dropped one and cut it after a minute — and you can only reach the settings on two of them. So you hum every twenty seconds. The hum carries no information and it is the only reason the call survives to hear the answer.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • four minutes of thinking = extended reasoning or a tool call, with no tokens on the wire

  • six switchboards = client SDK, corporate proxy, carrier NAT, CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy

  • "only two you can reach" = you configure the ALB and nginx; NAT and corporate proxies are not yours

  • the hum every twenty seconds = a : comment line, under half the shortest timeout on the path

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The three numbers

Heartbeat interval. interval < min(all idle timeouts on the path) / 2. Behind a 60-second ALB with mobile clients, 20–25 seconds. The factor of two exists so one lost heartbeat doesn't cost the connection.

Connection capacity. Fleet ceiling is nodes × per-node connection limit, and per-node is bounded by file descriptors and per-connection memory rather than CPU. At ~40 KB per connection, 50,000 connections is roughly 2 GB before any application state — which is why per-stream state should be an id and a buffer reference, not a rich object.

Drain and reconnect. Dropping C connections over a jitter window W against a fleet accepting A per second requires W > C/A. It also sets the drain window: to complete rather than sever generations, the grace period must exceed the p99 generation duration, and the orchestrator's termination grace must exceed that.

Why TCP keepalive is not the answer

Linux tcp_keepalive_time defaults to 7200 seconds — two hours before the first probe. That is useless as a liveness check for a connection that must survive a 60-second idle timer, and it is also the wrong layer: the middleboxes cutting your connection are counting application bytes, not TCP probes. Application-level heartbeats are the only mechanism that both keeps the path alive and detects a dead peer in a useful window.

What makes this domain different

An idle HTTP connection costs a socket. An idle AI connection costs a socket and a GPU slot working on a generation whose output has nowhere to go if the connection dies. That asymmetry changes every decision here: timeouts are raised more aggressively, drains are longer, per-generation buffers exist so a reconnect resumes rather than re-runs, and severed connections are measured in GPU-seconds rather than error counts.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is completed generations per attempt, and its inverse is money. Every connection severed mid-generation is GPU time already spent on output the user never saw, plus a user who re-asks and spends it again. At any meaningful scale that is a real line item, and it's invisible in error-rate dashboards because a client-side disconnect is not a server error.

The second observable is connection count, which is a different kind of number from request rate: it doesn't fall when traffic is quiet, it doesn't shed under load, and it sizes the fleet. Once you own it, capacity planning stops being about CPU and becomes about descriptors, memory, and how many connections a rollout can afford to sever — which is the question this section exists to answer.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

location /v1/stream {
    proxy_pass http://inference_gateway;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;      # default 60s — a 3-minute reasoning gap dies on the default
    proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
    send_timeout 3600s;            # applies between successive writes TO the client
}

# Heartbeat inside the generator: a comment line, emitted whenever the model is quiet.
async def gen():
    last = time.monotonic()
    async for tok in model.generate(prompt):          # may block for minutes on a tool call
        yield f"id: {seq}\ndata: {json.dumps(tok)}\n\n"
        last = time.monotonic()
    # a concurrent task emits ": ping\n\n" if now - last > 20s, so the path stays alive
    # 20s is under half of the 60s ALB / carrier-NAT floor — NOT near it

ss -tan state established '( sport = :8443 )' | wc -l   # live streams on this gateway
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_time                # 7200 — why it can't be your liveness check

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Scenario: 10 gateways × 5,000 streams; a generation with a 185-second tool-call gap; then a rolling deploy.

📥 [0.0s]  GET /v1/stream → gateway-3, generation g_8f2 starts
    │
    ▼
🎯 [0.4s]  first token → TTFT 400ms
    │
    ▼
🤔 [3s–185s] tool call: model produces nothing for 182 seconds
    │      ": ping" every 20s → 9 heartbeats, ~14 bytes each
    │      ALB idle timer, carrier NAT entry and corporate proxy all reset
    ▼
❌ [alt] with no heartbeat: ALB cuts at 60s → client sees a closed stream,
    │      model keeps generating for another 125s → 125 GPU-seconds wasted, no error logged
    ▼
✅ [185s] tokens resume; generation completes at 214s
    │
    ▼
🚀 [deploy] gateway-3 deregisters → 0 new streams; 5,000 in flight
    │      drain window 360s (p99 generation ≈ 300s) → 4,930 complete naturally
    ▼
📡 [+360s] 70 stragglers get {"type":"going_away","reconnect_after_ms":random(0,20000)}
    │      70 reconnects over 20s = 3.5/s against 9 nodes — trivial ✅
    ▼
🔄 [+362s] each resumes on a new node with Last-Event-ID → replays from the buffer

1. The nine heartbeats cost about 126 bytes and saved the generation. That is the entire mechanism, and it's why this is a configuration problem rather than an architecture problem for short generations — until you meet a hop you can't configure, which is what the heartbeat is actually for.

2. The alternative branch is the failure worth being able to describe. The ALB cut the connection; the model didn't know and kept working. No 5xx, no alert, no trace of the waste. The only way to see it is a metric that counts generations whose client vanished before completion, and the only way to price it is GPU-seconds attached to that count.

3. Draining to the p99 rather than to a fixed number is the design decision. A 60-second drain would have severed thousands of in-flight generations; 360 seconds severed 70. The cost is a slower rollout — ten nodes at six minutes each is an hour — and that trade should be stated explicitly rather than discovered when someone shortens it.

4. terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed the drain window. If the orchestrator's grace is 120 seconds and your drain is 360, the pod is killed at 120 and the drain was theatre. This mismatch is one of the most common self-inflicted versions of this failure.

5. The 70 stragglers reconnecting over 20 seconds is small because the drain did the work. At a 60-second drain it would have been thousands in the same window, which is where the W > C/A inequality starts to bite and where an un-jittered reconnect becomes a self-inflicted denial of service.

10. When TO Use This

  • Any streaming generation that can exceed 60 seconds — extended reasoning, tool use, long RAG pipelines, long-form output. The default timeouts on the path assume you finish inside a minute.

  • Any client on a mobile or corporate network — those are the hops you can't configure, and heartbeats are the only defence.

  • Any gateway tier holding thousands of concurrent streams — the sizing, the deploy story and the slow-consumer policy all follow from connection count rather than request rate.

  • Whenever a severed connection costs compute — which in this domain is always, and is what justifies longer drains and per-generation buffers.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't hold a connection for work measured in tens of minutes. Past a few minutes the odds of surviving every hop drop sharply and the value of live tokens falls. That's 202 and a job resource.

  • Don't raise timeouts and skip heartbeats. You control two hops out of six; the carrier NAT and the corporate proxy will still cut you, and the symptom will be "only some customers".

  • Don't use TCP keepalive as the liveness mechanism. Two hours of default idle time means you hold dead sessions — and their GPU work — for two hours.

  • Don't let the outbound queue grow unbounded. A slow reader plus an eager model is a memory-exhaustion bug with idle CPU and no errors. Bound it and disconnect-with-resume.

  • Don't shorten the drain window to speed up deploys. The saving is minutes of rollout; the cost is severed generations, wasted GPU-seconds and users re-asking. Put both numbers on the same slide before choosing.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "We raised the load-balancer idle timeout, so long generations are safe."

✅ Reality: You fixed the hops you own. The user's carrier NAT, their employer's proxy and their SDK's read timeout are all still on the path with their own limits. Heartbeats are what defend those, and the failure without them looks like "it only breaks for some customers", which is the hardest kind to diagnose.

❌ Misconception: "A dropped connection cancels the generation."

✅ Reality: A dropped TCP flow through NAT produces no FIN, so the server often learns seconds or minutes later, if at all. Generation continues and GPU time is spent for nobody. Cancellation on disconnect is a best-effort optimisation, not a guarantee — budget for the waste.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I set the heartbeat near the timeout — 55 seconds against a 60-second ALB — reasoning that fewer heartbeats meant less overhead. One delayed heartbeat under load and the connection died. The interval has to be under half the minimum, and the overhead being saved was fourteen bytes.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Naming one timeout. "We set the ALB to 4000 seconds" is a partial answer. Enumerate the path — SDK, corporate proxy, carrier NAT, CDN, LB, reverse proxy — and say which two you actually control.

Forgetting the reasoning gap. People design for token flow and never mention the minutes of silence during a tool call, which is exactly when the connection dies. Raising it unprompted signals you've operated one of these.

Treating a severed connection as free. In this domain it costs GPU-seconds already spent. If your answer doesn't attach a cost to disconnections, you've described a web service rather than an inference service.

Skipping the deploy. The largest disconnection event is scheduled and self-inflicted. Drain window, termination grace, jittered reconnect, resume-by-sequence — all four, or the design isn't finished.

Confusing connection count with request rate. They size different things. A streaming tier is sized by concurrent connections, and saying so is what shows you'd provision it correctly.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
AWS ALB idle timeout default 60s Applies to streaming connections; raise it explicitly AWS ELB docs
nginx proxy_read_timeout default 60s Between successive reads — a reasoning gap trips it nginx docs
Linux tcp_keepalive_time default 7200s Why TCP keepalive cannot be the liveness check Linux tcp(7)
Practical heartbeat interval 20–25s Under half the 60s path minimum Derived
SSE heartbeat form : comment line Ignored by the client parser; resets every idle timer WHATWG HTML §9.2
Reconnect dispersal W > C / A Jitter window must exceed connections ÷ accept rate AWS Architecture Blog
Full Jitter random(0, min(cap, base·2^n)) Beat plain and equal jitter on total work and completion time AWS Architecture Blog

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Heartbeats cost bytes, not latency; the real trade is drain length against rollout speed
💰 Cost The tier is sized by peak concurrent connections, so it costs the same at 3am; severed generations cost GPU-seconds on top
🔒 Security / visibility Long-lived connections sit outside per-request rate limiting, so abuse controls must be per-connection and per-tenant
📈 Scale Capacity is nodes × per-node connection ceiling; adding nodes doesn't relieve connections already placed
🔧 Ops complexity Every deploy, scale-in and zonal failover becomes a designed traffic event with a runbook
🐛 Debuggability The characteristic failures are silent — no errors, no latency change — so client-side delivery lag and severed-generation counts are mandatory, not optional

16. Real World Usage

Extended-reasoning and agentic products are why this item exists: a model that thinks for minutes or calls a tool produces exactly the silence that middleboxes treat as a dead connection, and heartbeats went from nice-to-have to load-bearing when those features shipped.

Provider APIs with long-running requests publish streaming as the recommended mode partly for this reason — a stream with regular events survives paths that a single long-blocking request does not.

Voice and realtime agents take the same constraints to the extreme, holding a bidirectional connection for the length of a conversation with per-session GPU state behind it, which makes drain windows and resumption a first-class design problem rather than an operational detail.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym. One term worth pinning: drain — deregistering a node from the load balancer so it accepts no new connections while continuing to serve existing ones. It is not the same as a graceful shutdown, which stops work; a drain deliberately keeps working while becoming invisible to new traffic.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 168-streaming-llm-tokens.md — the streaming path these connections carry

  • 27-keepalives-idle-timeouts.md — where the 60-second defaults come from

  • 73-websocket-operational-reality.md — the same operational problems for the bidirectional case

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 172-inference-load-balancing.md — how connections and requests are placed across replicas

  • 171-voice-agents.md — the extreme version, with per-session state and a hard latency budget

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • 202 + job resource — the right shape once generations outlast what the path will tolerate

  • Platform push — for a mobile client that will be backgrounded mid-generation

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Per-generation token buffer + Last-Event-ID — what turns a severed connection into a resume rather than a re-run

  • Connection draining and preStop hooks — how a rollout becomes gradual rather than instantaneous

  • Cross-folder: rollout strategy for long-lived connections → Section 13 (Kubernetes); backoff and jitter → 68-timeouts-retries-backoff.md

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Once a design includes streaming inference, this is the operational half of the round: "what happens when the model thinks for three minutes", "how do you deploy this", "what breaks at 50,000 concurrent streams". The strong answer enumerates the timeout path and names which hops are yours, sizes the tier by connections rather than requests, and treats the rollout as a rate-limited traffic event whose success metric is completed generations rather than restart time.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
5k concurrent streams fds and per-connection heap on the gateway Async runtime, raised ulimit -n/somaxconn, minimal per-stream state
50k concurrent streams Per-node connection ceiling; drain length vs rollout duration; slow-reader queues 10+ nodes, drain to p99 generation, bounded outbound queue with disconnect-and-resume
500k concurrent streams Deploy-time reconnect waves; single-region gateway tier Regional tiers, server-set jittered reconnect, connection-aware rollout with an auto-halt

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, the drain window multiplied by node count makes rollouts take hours, and someone shortens it without pricing the severed generations.

  • At 100x, per-generation buffers dominate memory before connection count does, because every in-flight generation holds its tokens twice.

  • Operationally, the 3am version is an autoscaler scaling in during a traffic dip: nodes terminated with no drain, thousands of generations severed, GPU time wasted, and the fleet scaling back out after the incident.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Severed generations per rollout, with GPU-seconds attached — the metric that makes the drain window a business decision.

  • Client-observed delivery lag and heartbeat gap — a connection that is open but silent past 2× the interval is functionally dead while every server metric stays green.

  • fd utilisation and accept-queue depth per gateway — alert well below the ceiling; this failure is a cliff, not a slope.

  • Outbound queue depth per connection, p99 — the slow-reader detector, minutes ahead of an OOM.
