notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Why media uses UDP, and what ICE/STUN/TURN do — WebRTC for the Curious: What, Why and How

  • Connectivity, candidates and the NAT traversal path — MDN: WebRTC connectivity

  • The protocol stack underneath — MDN: Introduction to WebRTC protocols

  • The full-duplex alternative — RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The end-to-end target for a natural turn? Under ~800 ms from end of speech to first audio out. Past ~1 s it reads as an awkward pause.
Why WebRTC rather than WebSocket for the audio leg? UDP with loss concealment — a late packet is worse than a lost one. TCP retransmits and adds head-of-line delay.
The stage that most often blows the budget? Endpointing — deciding the user has finished speaking. It's a deliberate delay, not a network one.
What is TURN for, and what does it cost? Relaying media when direct paths fail; it puts your servers in the media path and bills the bandwidth.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A voice turn is a pipeline with six stages: capture and encode, transport, speech-to-text with endpointing, LLM generation, text-to-speech, and playback with a jitter buffer. The budget from end-of-speech to first audio out is roughly 800 milliseconds, and each stage gets a slice. Transport is WebRTC over UDP rather than WebSocket over TCP, because for live audio a retransmitted packet arrives too late to be useful — you want loss concealment, not reliability. And the stage that usually eats the budget isn't the network at all: it's endpointing.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through the turn budget, stage by stage.

Capture and encode is 20–40 ms: the audio framing interval plus codec work, and it's mostly fixed by the frame size you chose. Transport is one-way network latency — 20–60 ms on a decent path within a region, and it's where geography shows up, because a cross-continent leg alone can exceed the entire remaining budget. Speech-to-text is streaming, so partial transcripts arrive continuously, but the finalised transcript waits on endpointing: the decision that the user has stopped talking, which is typically a silence threshold of a few hundred milliseconds and is the single largest controllable item.

Then LLM time-to-first-token, 200–500 ms depending on prompt length and queue, followed by text-to-speech first-audio, another 100–300 ms. Finally the jitter buffer and playback add 40–100 ms on the way back, because the receiver deliberately holds a small amount of audio to smooth out network variance.

Summed, a well-tuned pipeline lands around 700–900 ms from end of speech to first audio. The reason to hold the whole budget in your head is that every stage is owned by a different team, and the only way to know whose 200 ms to attack is to instrument all six.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

WebRTC or WebSocket for the audio transport?

WebRTC is the right default. Media rides UDP, so a lost packet is concealed rather than retransmitted — which is what you want, because audio that arrives 200 ms late is useless even if it's perfect. It brings adaptive bitrate, echo cancellation, jitter buffering and NAT traversal as solved problems, and it's what every browser already implements for real-time audio. The cost is a genuinely complex stack: signalling, SDP, ICE candidate gathering, and STUN/TURN infrastructure you have to run and pay for.

WebSocket carries audio over TCP, which means retransmission and head-of-line blocking: one lost segment stalls everything behind it, and on a lossy mobile link that turns into audible stutter and growing delay. What it buys is simplicity — one connection, ordinary TLS, no ICE, no TURN — and it's genuinely fine for server-to-server audio on a reliable network, or for a prototype where you'd rather not run coturn.

The line I'd hold: browser or mobile client on a real network is WebRTC, and the extra infrastructure is the price of not shipping stutter. Server-to-server, or a controlled network where loss is negligible, WebSocket is defensible. What isn't defensible is choosing WebSocket for a consumer voice product because WebRTC looked complicated, then discovering the complexity again as jitter bugs.

4. Quick Comparison Table

WebRTC WebSocket audio HTTP + SSE
Transport UDP (SRTP), DTLS TCP, TLS TCP, TLS
Loss behaviour conceal, keep going retransmit, head-of-line stall retransmit
NAT traversal ICE/STUN/TURN, solved ordinary outbound TCP ordinary outbound
Extra infrastructure signalling + STUN/TURN none none
Upstream audio ✅ native ✅ ❌ one-way
When you'd actually pick it consumer voice on real networks server-to-server, controlled links, prototypes the text half only

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The budget, written down

turn_latency = capture + transport_up + endpointing + STT_finalise + LLM_TTFT + TTS_first_audio + transport_down + jitter_buffer

A representative allocation: 30 + 40 + 300 + 40 + 260 + 150 + 40 + 60 ≈ 920 ms, which is already at the edge of feeling natural. That sum is why the design conversation is about removing stages rather than speeding each up: overlapping TTS with LLM generation (start speaking the first sentence while the rest generates) removes most of the TTS term, and aggressive endpointing with barge-in recovery removes most of the largest term.

Two structural facts follow. Geography is fatal: a cross-continent leg at 150 ms one-way appears twice and consumes a third of the budget, so voice pipelines are regional or they don't meet the target. Barge-in must be supported: the user interrupting has to cancel generation and playback within tens of milliseconds, which is why the upstream and downstream legs are usually on one connection — coordinating a cancellation across two is a race you will lose.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't run the media leg over TCP for a consumer product. Retransmission plus head-of-line blocking on a lossy mobile link produces stutter and growing delay, and no amount of buffering fixes it — the buffer is the delay.

  • Don't skip TURN and hope direct paths work. A meaningful share of clients sit behind NATs and firewalls where only a relay connects. Without TURN those users simply fail, and they'll be the ones on corporate networks.

  • Don't split upstream audio and downstream tokens across two connections without an interruption plan. Barge-in becomes a cross-connection race, and the user hears the agent talking over them.

  • Don't put the model in another region. Two 150 ms legs consume a third of the turn budget before any computation, and there is no protocol fix for the speed of light.

  • Don't optimise the network before measuring endpointing. The silence threshold is usually the largest single term and it's a product decision, not a networking one.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Voice latency is a network problem."

✅ Reality: In a well-built pipeline the network legs are 60–100 ms of an 800 ms budget. Endpointing, LLM TTFT and TTS first-audio dominate. The network matters enormously in one specific way — cross-region placement — and barely at all otherwise.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated TURN as a fallback that would rarely fire, so its bandwidth wasn't in the cost model. It fires for a substantial minority of real users, it puts your servers in the media path for the whole call, and relayed audio is billed as egress — which makes it a capacity and cost component, not an edge case.

📚 Reference Links

  • Inference-aware routing as a standard — Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension

  • Why a normal LB is the wrong shape here — Kubernetes blog: Introducing Gateway API Inference Extension

  • What cache locality is actually worth — vLLM: Automatic Prefix Caching

  • Load-balancing algorithms, as implemented — Envoy: Load balancing — supported algorithms

  • Bonus — Google SRE Book: Handling Overload

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why does round-robin hurt inference? Requests have wildly unequal cost and replicas have unequal cache state. Equal counts ≠ equal load.
The signal that actually correlates with load? Queue depth (or KV-cache utilisation) reported by the model server — not connections, not requests.
What does prefix affinity buy? A cache hit on a shared prompt prefix, collapsing prefill from hundreds of ms to near zero.
Why does an L4 balancer fail outright? It balances connections; gRPC/HTTP2 multiplexes everything onto one, so one replica takes it all.
What is the endpoint picker? The Inference Extension component that chooses a replica using model-server metrics, per request.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Ordinary load balancing assumes requests cost roughly the same and backends are interchangeable. Neither holds for inference: one request may be 200 prompt tokens and another 20,000, and a replica that already holds your prompt's prefix in its KV cache can answer far faster than an idle one. So round-robin spreads work evenly by count and unevenly by load, and it actively destroys cache locality. The right router reads queue depth and cache state from the model servers and routes on that, with affinity for shared prefixes — which is what the Gateway API Inference Extension standardises.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why exactly does round-robin hurt, when it's fine for stateless HTTP?

Two assumptions break. Uniform request cost: for a normal service, requests are within an order of magnitude of each other, so equal counts approximate equal load. In inference, prefill scales with prompt length and decode with output length, so a 20,000-token RAG request and a 200-token chat turn differ by two orders of magnitude in GPU work. Round-robin gives each replica the same number of requests and wildly different work — some queues back up while others idle, and the balancer's metrics look perfect because it's counting the thing it balanced.

Interchangeable backends: model servers are stateful in a way that matters. The KV cache holds attention state for tokens already processed, and prefix caching lets a replica that recently served the same system prompt skip recomputing it. Sending the next turn to a random replica throws that away and pays full prefill again, so correct placement depends on what each replica already knows — exactly what a generic balancer can't see.

Put together: the router needs per-replica load (queue depth, batch occupancy, KV-cache utilisation) and per-replica affinity (which prefixes it holds), neither of which is visible at L4 or in a plain L7 request count.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Least-request, queue-depth-aware, or prefix affinity?

Least-request — send to the replica with the fewest in-flight requests — is the cheap improvement over round-robin and it's the right first move. It's a decent proxy for load when request costs vary, requires nothing from the backend, and every mature proxy implements it. Its weakness is that "in flight" doesn't distinguish a request that's about to finish decoding from one that just started a 20,000-token prefill, so it degrades exactly when the cost spread is widest.

Queue-depth routing asks the model server how loaded it actually is — pending requests, batch occupancy, KV-cache utilisation — and routes on that. Strictly better, because it uses the signal that causes the latency, and it's what the Inference Extension's endpoint picker is built around. The cost is a control loop: stale metrics produce herding, where every router sees the same "least loaded" replica and stampedes it.

Prefix affinity routes by what a replica already holds, and it's the largest single win when there's a shared prefix — a long system prompt, a multi-turn conversation, a document asked about repeatedly — converting hundreds of milliseconds of prefill into near zero. Its risk is hot-spotting.

The production answer is layered rather than chosen: affinity first, bounded by a load ceiling, falling back to queue-depth routing when the preferred replica is saturated. Stating it as "affinity with a load cap" is a much stronger answer than naming any single algorithm.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

One conversation becomes enormously popular. What happens, and what runs out?

📍 Seen in the wild: the hot-key question, and the one that exposes pure affinity.

With prefix affinity, popularity concentrates: every request sharing that prefix routes to the replica holding it, so one GPU saturates while the fleet idles. What runs out first is that replica's KV-cache memory and batch slots — the cache is finite, so beyond a point it evicts the very prefix that made it preferred, and you get the worst of both worlds: a hot replica and cache misses. Queue depth on that replica climbs, TTFT for those users spikes, and every fleet-average metric stays healthy.

The mitigations are the standard hot-key ones, adapted. Cap affinity with a load threshold so the router abandons the preferred replica above a queue bound — accepting a cache miss to avoid a queue. Replicate the hot prefix across a small set of replicas and balance within it, the direct analogue of replicating a hot shard. And separate traffic classes so long-prompt requests can't starve short interactive turns.

It presents as p99 TTFT rising for a subset of users while p50 is unchanged and fleet GPU utilisation looks fine — the signature of concentration, exposed only by per-replica queue depth plotted as a distribution.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the routing layer for a multi-model inference platform on Kubernetes.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that a normal Service is the wrong primitive here, and why.

The highest-stakes constraint is that a Kubernetes Service balances at L4, per connection, and inference traffic runs over HTTP/2 with long-lived multiplexed connections — so one client pins to one replica for the connection's life and adding replicas does nothing. That single fact rules out the default primitive before any algorithm discussion, and it's the thing to say first.

So the data path is an L7 gateway with an inference-aware routing extension: the gateway terminates HTTP/2, and for each request an endpoint picker consults live model-server metrics — queue depth, KV-cache utilisation, which adapters or prefixes are loaded — and returns a replica. That's what the Gateway API Inference Extension's InferencePool and endpoint picker provide, and adopting the standard matters more than the specific implementation because it keeps the routing policy out of every client.

Around it, three things: traffic classes with their own pools so long-prompt and interactive traffic don't share a queue; admission control at the gateway — 429 with Retry-After when the pool is saturated, since queueing indefinitely turns a capacity problem into a timeout problem for everyone; and model-aware routing when several models or adapters share a fleet, because a request for a model a replica hasn't loaded is an error, not a slow route.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is per-replica queue-depth skew, not average utilisation — skew is what reveals stale routing signal or concentrating affinity, and both look healthy at fleet level.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Algorithm Signal used Handles cost variance Preserves cache Failure mode When you'd actually pick it
Round-robin none ❌ ❌ uneven queues, balanced-looking metrics Never, for inference
L4 / connection-based connections ❌ accidental one replica takes everything over h2 Never, for inference
Least-request in-flight count partly ❌ can't tell a starting 20k prefill from a finishing decode The cheap first improvement
Queue-depth / metrics-aware model-server queue, KV utilisation ✅ ❌ by itself herding on stale metrics The default for a serious fleet
Prefix / session affinity which replica holds the prefix ❌ alone ✅ hot-spotting on a popular prefix Layer it on top, with a load cap
Affinity + load cap (layered) both ✅ ✅ more moving parts What production converges on

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

Design axis: how much does the router know about what each kitchen is currently doing, and what it has already prepped?

📖 Story — one order, four ways to pick a kitchen

  • Round-robin. Hand the next order to the next kitchen in the rota. Works if every dish takes the same time. One kitchen gets a banquet, the next gets a sandwich, and the rota says they're even.

  • Least-request. Give it to whoever has fewest orders on the pass. Better — until you can't tell that one of those orders is a banquet just started and the other is a sandwich being plated.

  • Queue depth. Ask each kitchen how backed up it actually is and believe the answer. Right signal — but if you ask everyone at once and they all name the same quiet kitchen, you send them all there.

  • Affinity. Send it to the kitchen that already prepped this exact base sauce this morning. Enormously faster — until that sauce becomes popular and one kitchen is buried while three stand idle.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • the banquet and the sandwich = a 20,000-token prefill and a 200-token turn on the same rota

  • "the rota says they're even" = a load balancer counting the thing it balanced

  • "they all name the same quiet kitchen" = herding on stale metrics

  • the prepped base sauce = a KV-cache prefix hit, and the buried kitchen is the hot-spot it creates

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Why "balanced" is the wrong word

A normal balancer optimises for equal request counts; what you want is equal time-to-drain, and the two diverge as soon as cost varies. If replica A holds one 20,000-token prefill and replica B holds five 200-token turns, B has five times the requests and a fraction of the work. Queue depth measured in pending work — the model server's own view of batch occupancy and KV utilisation — is the signal that correlates with the latency you're controlling.

The cache-locality arithmetic

Prefill cost scales with prompt tokens. If a shared system prompt is p tokens and the user turn is u tokens, a cold replica computes p + u and a replica holding the prefix computes roughly u. With p = 2,000 and u = 100, that's a ~95% reduction in prefill work for that request — which is why affinity is worth building a router around rather than treating as an optimisation. Expressed as a routing rule: a cache hit is worth a meaningful amount of queue, so the affinity cap should be set in terms of expected wait versus prefill saved, not as an arbitrary threshold.

Herding, and why freshness matters

Metrics-based routing is a control loop with delay. If every router sees a snapshot d seconds old and N requests arrive within d, all N go to whatever was least loaded at snapshot time — which is now the most loaded. Standard fixes: sample a small random subset and pick the best of it ("power of two choices"), refresh metrics fast relative to arrival rate, and add a random tiebreak among near-equal candidates.

Admission control belongs here

When every replica is saturated, routing has nothing left to choose, and queueing further only converts a capacity problem into a timeout problem — clients wait, time out, retry, and amplify the overload. Shed with 429 and Retry-After at the one place that can see the whole pool.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is GPU utilisation versus TTFT, and the gap between them is what bad routing costs. A fleet can sit at 55% average utilisation with a p99 TTFT that looks like it's at 95%, because the work is concentrated and the average is hiding it. That's capacity you've bought and aren't using, on the most expensive hardware in the system — which makes routing one of the highest-leverage things to fix in an inference platform, ahead of most model-level optimisation.

The second reason is that cache locality makes routing a cost decision, not only a latency one. Prefill you avoid is compute you don't buy, so a router that preserves prefix hits on long shared system prompts changes the effective capacity of the same fleet — without touching the model, the framework, or the prompts.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Gateway API Inference Extension: the pool is the routing unit, and the
# endpoint picker — not the Service — chooses the replica per request.
apiVersion: inference.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: InferencePool
metadata:
  name: chat-pool
spec:
  selector:
    app: vllm-chat                 # the replicas; NOT fronted by a normal ClusterIP Service,
                                   # because L4 would pin each HTTP/2 connection to one pod
  targetPortNumber: 8000
  extensionRef:
    name: chat-endpoint-picker     # reads queue depth / KV utilisation / loaded adapters
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: chat-route
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: inference-gateway }]
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - group: inference.networking.k8s.io
          kind: InferencePool       # route to the POOL, so the picker runs per request
          name: chat-pool

# The diagnostic that exposes the whole problem: distribution, not average.
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep -E 'num_requests_waiting|gpu_cache_usage_perc'
# Healthy: queue depths clustered. Broken: one replica at 40 while others sit at 0.

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Scenario: 8 replicas, a 2,000-token shared system prompt, mixed traffic — 90% short turns, 10% long RAG requests.

📥 [1] request A: 2,000-token shared prefix + 120-token turn, conversation c_9f
    │
    ▼
🔎 [2] picker: replica-3 holds prefix p_9f (served c_9f 40s ago), queue 1 → under cap
    │
    ▼
🎯 [3] routed to replica-3: prefill ≈ 120 tokens, not 2,120 → 14ms instead of 168ms
    │      TTFT 191ms
    ▼
📥 [4] request B: 18,000-token RAG prompt, no cached prefix
    │
    ▼
⚖️ [5] picker: no affinity; lowest queue is replica-6 (queue 0) → routed there
    │      prefill 1.4s; replica-6's queue depth reported as 1 but its WORK is huge
    ▼
❌ [6] round-robin comparison for the same minute:
    │      replica-3 cache hit rate 71% → 9%; mean prefill 22ms → 151ms
    │      queue-depth spread across replicas: 0–2 → 0–11
    │      fleet GPU utilisation 61% both ways; p99 TTFT 340ms → 1.9s
    ▼
🔥 [7] c_9f goes viral: 600 rps share prefix p_9f
    │      pure affinity → replica-3 queue hits 40, KV evicts p_9f, cache hit rate collapses
    ▼
✅ [8] with a load cap: picker abandons replica-3 above queue 8, spreads to 4 replicas
       that each warm p_9f → hit rate 68%, max queue 9, p99 TTFT back to 410ms

1. Step 3 is the whole affinity argument in one number. 168 ms of prefill became 14 ms because the replica already held the prefix. On a 2,000-token system prompt that's a ~95% reduction in prefill work, repeated on every request in the conversation, and it comes purely from where you sent it.

2. Step 5 shows why in-flight count is a weak signal. replica-6 had queue depth 0 and was about to spend 1.4 seconds on prefill; anything routed there next sits behind it. Queue depth weighted by pending tokens is better still — which is why the model server's own metrics beat anything a proxy can infer.

3. Step 6 is the comparison worth memorising. Identical hardware, identical traffic, identical fleet-average GPU utilisation — and a p99 TTFT nearly six times worse. Average utilisation is the metric that hides this completely, which is why per-replica queue-depth spread belongs on the dashboard instead.

4. Step 7 is affinity failing in the specific way affinity fails. Concentration creates a queue and blows the cache on the replica you relied on, so you lose the benefit you concentrated for. Both arrive together.

5. Step 8 is the layered answer working. A load cap converts affinity from "always the same replica" into "one of a few warm replicas", which is the hot-shard replication pattern. Hit rate barely moved; the queue and the tail came back under control.

10. When TO Use This

  • Any self-hosted inference fleet with more than a couple of replicas — the gap between round-robin and metrics-aware routing shows up immediately in p99 TTFT.

  • Workloads with a long shared prefix — a large system prompt, a RAG document reused across questions, multi-turn conversations. This is where affinity pays the most.

  • Mixed-cost traffic — short chat turns alongside long-context requests on the same fleet. Without cost-aware routing (or separate pools) the long requests set everyone's tail latency.

  • Multi-model or multi-adapter fleets — routing must be model-aware, because a request for a model a replica hasn't loaded isn't a slow route, it's a failed one.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't build inference-aware routing for a single replica. There's nothing to choose between; spend the effort on batching and prompt length.

  • Don't use a plain Kubernetes Service for HTTP/2 inference traffic. It balances connections, so each client pins to one replica and scaling out changes nothing. This is the first thing to check, not the last.

  • Don't run pure affinity without a load cap. A popular prefix concentrates traffic onto one replica and then evicts the very cache that made it attractive.

  • Don't route on stale metrics without a randomised choice. Every router seeing the same snapshot sends everything to the same "least loaded" replica. Power-of-two-choices exists for this.

  • Don't let the router queue indefinitely when the pool is saturated. Shed with 429 and Retry-After — an unbounded queue turns a capacity shortfall into fleet-wide timeouts and a retry storm.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Round-robin is fine — the requests average out."

✅ Reality: They average out in count, not in work. With two orders of magnitude of cost spread between a short turn and a long-context request, equal counts produce wildly unequal queues, and the load balancer's own metrics report perfect balance because it's counting the thing it balanced.

❌ Misconception: "Session affinity is a stickiness feature for correctness."

✅ Reality: Here it's a performance and cost feature. Nothing breaks if the next turn goes elsewhere — you just pay full prefill again. That reframing matters, because it means affinity is negotiable under load, which is exactly what a load cap exploits.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I judged the fleet by average GPU utilisation. It sat around 60% and looked like headroom, while p99 TTFT said we were saturated — because the work was concentrated on two replicas. The metric that mattered was the spread of per-replica queue depth, and no average would ever have shown it.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Naming an algorithm without naming the signal. "Least-request" is a mechanism; the discussion is about what correlates with load here, which is queue depth and KV utilisation reported by the model server. Lead with the signal.

Forgetting the L4 problem. If the design puts a normal Service in front of HTTP/2 inference traffic, everything downstream of that is moot. It's the highest-value thing to say first and it's frequently skipped.

Treating cache locality as an optimisation. On long shared prefixes it's the dominant term in prefill. Presenting it as a nice-to-have understates it by an order of magnitude.

No answer for the hot prefix. Anyone who proposes affinity will be asked what happens when one prefix gets popular. "Load cap plus deliberate replication" is the answer; silence suggests you've only read about it.

Skipping admission control. Routing has no answer when every replica is full. Saying so — and shedding with 429 and Retry-After — is what separates a routing design from a queueing accident.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Prefill cost scales with prompt tokens A cached prefix collapses it to the new tokens only vLLM prefix-caching docs
Routing unit InferencePool + endpoint picker Per-request selection using model-server metrics Gateway API Inference Extension
Key model-server signals pending queue, KV-cache utilisation, loaded adapters What the picker reads Gateway API Inference Extension
K8s Service balancing L4, per connection Pins HTTP/2 multiplexed traffic to one replica Kubernetes networking model
Power of two choices sample 2, pick better Most of the benefit of global knowledge, without herding Envoy LB docs
Utilisation knee ~70–80% Past it, queue wait rises sharply for the same arrival rate Queueing theory
Shed signal 429 + Retry-After The correct response to a saturated pool RFC 6585, RFC 9110 §10.2.3

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Affinity buys prefill time; a load cap trades some cache hits for a shorter queue — the cap is where you set that exchange rate
💰 Cost Better routing raises effective capacity on hardware you already own; avoided prefill is compute you don't buy
🔒 Security / visibility Per-request routing at L7 means the gateway sees payload metadata (model, tenant, prompt length) — useful for policy, and a place where prompts can leak into logs
📈 Scale Metrics-based routing is a control loop; its accuracy degrades as request rate outpaces metric freshness
🔧 Ops complexity An endpoint picker is another component on the critical path of every request, with its own failure and upgrade story
🐛 Debuggability Per-replica queue depth and cache hit rate must be exported and graphed as distributions; averages actively conceal every failure in this note

16. Real World Usage

The Gateway API Inference Extension exists because this problem is universal enough to standardise: an InferencePool plus an endpoint picker that routes on live model-server metrics, rather than a Service that routes on connections. Being able to name it and say what it replaces is the fastest way to show you've kept up with this area.

Self-hosted vLLM fleets are where prefix caching and queue-depth routing were first combined in practice, because the framework exports exactly the signals the router needs — waiting requests and KV-cache utilisation.

Multi-tenant platforms serving many LoRA adapters push the model-aware case hardest: routing must consider which adapters a replica has loaded, since a replica lacking the adapter means a load-and-wait or an error, not a slightly slower route.

17. Acronym Decoder

KV cache — key/value cache: the stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, so they aren't recomputed. Worth decoding because the name explains the routing consequence — it's per-replica state, which is what makes replicas non-interchangeable. EPP — endpoint picker, the Inference Extension component that selects a replica per request. TTFT — time to first token, the latency this routing exists to protect.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 169-time-to-first-token.md — queue wait and prefill are the terms routing attacks

  • 93-grpc-in-production.md — the same connection-pinning problem, in its general form

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 177-multi-tenant-isolation.md — per-tenant limits on top of the same routing layer

  • 176-cost-and-data-path.md — where the GPU traffic actually flows and what it costs

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Separate pools per traffic class — often simpler and nearly as effective as clever routing

  • Client-side load balancing — removes a hop, at the cost of putting model-server metrics into every client

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Admission control and 429 + Retry-After — what routing does when there's nothing good left to choose

  • Prefix caching in the serving framework — routing only preserves locality that the framework can exploit

  • Cross-folder: continuous batching, KV cache and prefill/decode split → LLM folder (serving); HPA on GPU metrics → Section 13

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

"Design the serving layer for a self-hosted model fleet" reaches this within a few minutes, and it's the item that most separates people who've operated inference from people who've operated web services. The strong answer rejects the default Service for a stated reason, names queue depth and KV utilisation as the routing signal, layers affinity with a load cap, and has an answer for the hot prefix and for a saturated pool. It's also the place where fleet-average utilisation gets called out as the metric that hides everything.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
8 replicas Round-robin destroys cache locality; L4 pinning Endpoint picker on queue depth + prefix affinity with a load cap
100 replicas Metric freshness vs request rate → herding Power-of-two-choices sampling, faster metric refresh, randomised tiebreak
1000 replicas, multi-region Global prefix map becomes its own scaling problem; cross-region routing costs RTT Shard the prefix map, keep routing region-local, replicate hot prefixes deliberately

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, per-replica queue-depth skew becomes the dominant latency effect while fleet-average utilisation still reads as healthy headroom.

  • At 100x, the endpoint picker's metric pipeline is the bottleneck, and stale snapshots produce herding that looks like random tail-latency spikes.

  • Operationally, the 3am version is a popular conversation or shared document concentrating traffic onto one replica, evicting the cache it was routed for, and spiking p99 for one cohort while every fleet metric stays green.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Per-replica queue depth as a distribution (p50/p99 and max/min skew) — the single most revealing metric in this note; averages hide every failure here.

  • Prefix-cache hit rate, per pool — falling hit rate means the router lost locality, and prefill cost rises immediately behind it.

  • TTFT p99 split by pool and prompt-length band — catches long-context traffic starving interactive traffic.

  • Shed rate (429) and the queue depth at which it triggers — admission control that never fires is either over-provisioned or misconfigured, and both are worth knowing.

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Rate limits and the headers a provider returns — Claude Docs: Rate limits

  • Error classes and which are retryable — Claude Docs: API errors

  • Retry-After semantics (normative) — RFC 9110 §10.2.3

  • Full Jitter, with the simulation behind it — AWS Architecture Blog: Exponential Backoff And Jitter

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which provider errors are retryable? 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 529-style overload, connect errors and timeouts. Never 400/401/403/422.
What must you honour before your own backoff? The Retry-After header. Your exponential curve is the fallback, not the override.
Why does a streaming request need a different timeout? Total-duration timeouts are meaningless; use time-to-first-token plus an inter-token gap timeout.
What makes a retried generation safe and cheap? An idempotency key — otherwise a retry after a lost response is a second billed generation.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Calling an LLM provider is calling a shared, rate-limited, occasionally overloaded dependency whose responses take seconds and stream. So the retry policy needs three things a normal HTTP client doesn't have: timeouts expressed as time-to-first-token and inter-token gap rather than total duration, because a total timeout either kills long generations or never fires; Retry-After honoured ahead of your own backoff, because the provider knows when capacity returns; and an idempotency key, because a retry after a lost response is a second generation you pay for twice.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What timeout do you set on a streaming completion?

Not a total-duration one. A generation might legitimately run for three minutes, so a total timeout long enough to permit that is far too long to detect a stall — you'd wait three minutes to notice a dead connection. Instead, set two: a time-to-first-token timeout, typically a few seconds, which catches a queued or wedged request early; and an inter-token gap timeout, typically 15–30 seconds, which catches a stream that started and stopped. Together they detect failure in seconds while allowing arbitrarily long healthy generations.

A connect timeout sits underneath both and should be short — a second or two — because failing to establish a connection is a different failure from a slow provider and deserves a faster retry. And note that these are client-side timeouts on a connection that may pass through your own proxies, whose idle timeouts must be longer than your inter-token gap or they'll fire first and you'll misattribute the failure to the provider.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A provider returns 429 with Retry-After: 30. Do you wait, or fail over?

Waiting is correct when the request can tolerate the delay and the limit is genuinely transient — a burst you caused, clearing in seconds. Honouring Retry-After is not politeness, it's the only signal you have about when capacity returns, and ignoring it in favour of an aggressive exponential curve makes the queue longer for everyone including you, which is how a rate limit becomes an outage.

Failing over to a second provider or a smaller model is correct when the request is user-facing and 30 seconds is unacceptable. The costs are real and worth naming: different providers produce different outputs, so quality varies per request in a way users may notice; prompt formats and tool-calling schemas differ enough that a failover path is a second integration to maintain and test; and a failover path exercised only during incidents is a path that doesn't work during incidents.

My default is a tiered response rather than a binary one: honour Retry-After for background and batch work; for interactive traffic, retry once with jitter and then fail over to a fallback model, with the fallback exercised continuously by routing a small percentage of normal traffic to it. And crucially, cap total retries as a fraction of successful traffic rather than per request — a retry budget — because per-request caps still let a provider-wide incident multiply your load exactly when the provider can least absorb it.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Situation Signal Right response Wrong response
Rate limited 429 + Retry-After wait as instructed; shed or queue background work immediate retry, or your own shorter backoff
Provider overloaded 503 / overload error retry with full jitter, then fail over tight retry loop — amplifies the incident
Bad request 400 / 422 fail fast, surface it retry — it will never succeed
Auth failure 401 / 403 fail fast, alert retry — burns budget, may lock the key
Stream stalls mid-generation inter-token gap exceeded abandon, retry with the idempotency key wait for a total timeout that's minutes away
Lost response after submit connect error / timeout retry with the SAME idempotency key plain retry — a second billed generation

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic that makes retries dangerous here

Two multipliers stack. Layer amplification: three layers each retrying three times is 27× worst-case load on the provider — the standard result, and it applies with full force when your gateway, your SDK and your application each have their own retry logic. Retry at exactly one layer.

Cost amplification is specific to this domain. A normal retry costs a request; an LLM retry costs a generation — tokens billed, GPU time consumed. A retry of a partially-streamed response that already produced 800 tokens throws those away and pays again. That makes two things load-bearing: an idempotency key so a retry after a lost response resumes or returns the original rather than starting fresh, and abandoning on inter-token gap rather than letting a stalled stream run to a long total timeout while still being billed.

The control that bounds both is a retry budget — cap retries at, say, 10% of successful requests over a rolling window and shed beyond it. Per-request limits ("3 attempts") don't bound aggregate load during a provider incident; a budget does, and it's what stops your client from being part of the outage.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't retry 400, 401, 403 or 422. They are deterministic. Retrying wastes budget, delays the real error, and on auth failures can trigger lockouts.

  • Don't set a single total-duration timeout on a streaming call. Long enough for a legitimate generation means minutes before you notice a stall. Use TTFT plus inter-token gap.

  • Don't retry at every layer. SDK, gateway and application each retrying turns one failure into dozens. Pick one layer and disable the others explicitly.

  • Don't ignore Retry-After in favour of your own curve. The provider is telling you when capacity returns; overriding it lengthens the outage for everyone, including you.

  • Don't build a failover path you never exercise. A fallback model that's only used during incidents is untested during incidents. Route a small share of normal traffic through it.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Retries are cheap, so retry aggressively."

✅ Reality: An LLM retry re-runs a generation — tokens billed, GPU consumed, and a partially-streamed response's work discarded. Cost amplification is on top of the usual load amplification, which is why a retry budget rather than a per-request attempt limit is the right control.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated 429 as a failure to route around. It's a scheduling instruction with a number attached. Honouring Retry-After and shedding background work at that moment recovers faster than failing over, because failover moves the same load onto a second provider that is often correlated with the first.

notes.html:
🧭 Index amendment. The index line lists MCP transports as "stdio vs HTTP+SSE vs streamable HTTP". The current specification revision defines two standard bindings — stdio and Streamable HTTP; the separate HTTP+SSE transport belongs to earlier revisions and survives only for backward compatibility. Same amendment as Section 10, Item 99.

📚 Reference Links

  • The two standard bindings, normatively — Model Context Protocol: Transports

  • The private ranges an agent's egress check must deny — RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets

  • The metadata endpoint SSRF targets — AWS: Use the Instance Metadata Service

  • The SSE mechanics a Streamable HTTP server inherits — WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two current MCP transports? stdio (subprocess, standard streams) and Streamable HTTP (POST to one endpoint, reply JSON or an SSE stream).
What authenticates a stdio MCP server? Process ownership. There is no network surface, no port, no token.
Why is a URL-fetching tool an SSRF primitive? The destination is chosen by model output, so an attacker who influences the prompt chooses your outbound requests.
First thing to block on the egress path? The cloud metadata endpoint — link-local, unauthenticated, and holds instance credentials.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An agent's tool calls are network calls, and that changes the threat model. MCP gives two transports: stdio, where the client launches the server as a subprocess and identity is process ownership, and Streamable HTTP, where each message is a POST to one endpoint and the reply may be a request-scoped SSE stream — an ordinary internet-facing service with all that implies. The new risk is that a tool which fetches a URL takes its destination from model output, so anyone who can influence the prompt can direct your server's outbound requests. That's server-side request forgery with a language model choosing the target.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

stdio or Streamable HTTP — what actually differs at the network layer?

stdio has no network layer. The client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over its standard streams, so there's no port, no TLS, no listener, and no authentication beyond who owns the process. That makes it right for capabilities on the user's own machine — a filesystem, a local database, a git checkout — and it means the security question is process sandboxing rather than network policy. Its limits follow: one client per process, lifecycle tied to the parent, unreachable from anywhere else.

Streamable HTTP is a real service: one endpoint, each message a POST, and a reply that is either a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream when the server has progressive output. Everything HTTP gives you applies — TLS, bearer tokens or OAuth, gateways, rate limits, horizontal scaling — and so does everything HTTP costs you: proxy buffering on the streaming path, idle timeouts, tenancy, abuse controls, and an attack surface that is now reachable from wherever it's exposed.

The decision is about where the capability lives, not about preference. Local machine access is stdio. A shared service several users or agents call is Streamable HTTP, and at that point it needs authentication, per-tenant limits and an abuse story designed rather than assumed.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

An agent needs to fetch arbitrary web pages. How do you allow that safely?

The naive version — pass the model's URL to an HTTP client in your service — is a full SSRF primitive. The service typically sits in a private subnet with an IAM role, so a fetch of the link-local metadata address returns instance credentials, and a fetch of an internal hostname reaches services that trust network position instead of authenticating. The model doesn't need to be malicious for this; a poisoned web page telling it to fetch an internal URL is enough, which is why "the model wouldn't do that" is not a control.

The workable design routes every agent-initiated fetch through a dedicated egress proxy in its own network segment with no IAM role and no route to your VPC. The proxy resolves the hostname itself, checks the resolved address against a deny list of private, link-local, loopback and metadata ranges, then connects — and re-checks on redirects, because a public URL that 302s to an internal one defeats a name-only check. It also caps response size and time, and strips inbound headers that could carry credentials outward.

The residual risk worth naming is DNS rebinding: a hostname that resolves to a public address at check time and a private one at connect time. The fix is to connect to the address you validated rather than re-resolving, which most HTTP clients will not do for you and which is the detail that separates a real control from a checkbox.

4. Quick Comparison Table

stdio Streamable HTTP Local HTTP on loopback
Network surface none full internet-facing service host-local only
Identity process ownership OAuth / bearer, gateway-enforced whoever can reach loopback
Multi-user ❌ one client per process ✅ ❌
Streaming line-delimited messages request-scoped SSE SSE
Main risk subprocess escape, local file access tenancy, abuse, SSRF via tools any local process can call it
When you'd actually pick it user-machine capabilities shared capabilities dev only

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The three failure classes, all inherited from HTTP

Buffering. A Streamable HTTP server whose reply is an SSE stream is subject to every buffering hop in Section 168 — a proxy holding the stream turns progressive tool output into a single dump, with identical status codes and byte counts.

Idle timeouts. A tool call that takes minutes produces a silent connection, which a 60-second load-balancer default treats as dead. The MCP layer doesn't change that; heartbeats and raised timeouts do.

Cancellation. When the client abandons a request — on stdio a notifications/cancelled, on Streamable HTTP closing the response stream — the server may not learn for some time, because a dropped TCP flow produces no FIN. Tool work continues and resources are spent. Treat cancellation as best-effort and bound tool execution with its own deadline.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't expose a remote MCP server without treating it as a public service. It has an endpoint, tenants, authentication and abuse potential like any API. "It's just a tool server" is how an internal capability ends up internet-reachable.

  • Don't let a fetching tool use your service's own network identity. If the fetch runs in a process with an IAM role and a route into your VPC, one poisoned page is a credential disclosure.

  • Don't validate URLs by hostname or scheme alone. Validation must be on the resolved address, re-checked after every redirect, and the connection must go to the address you validated — otherwise DNS rebinding walks straight through.

  • Don't run stdio servers unsandboxed because "it's local". The subprocess inherits the user's filesystem access and environment. Local is a different threat model, not an absent one.

  • Don't let a tool call run without its own deadline. Cancellation is best-effort, so the tool's timeout is the only reliable bound on the work it consumes.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "MCP has three transports: stdio, HTTP+SSE and Streamable HTTP."

✅ Reality: The current spec defines two — stdio and Streamable HTTP. HTTP+SSE was a separate transport in earlier revisions and now exists only for backward compatibility. Streamable HTTP still uses SSE, as the response form for a streaming request, which is where the confusion comes from.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought prompt injection was a model-safety problem. The network consequence is what makes it severe: a poisoned page can direct the agent's outbound requests, so the mitigation isn't only better prompting, it's an egress path with no credentials and no route to anything that trusts network position.

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
What exactly does a safe egress check look like?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Allowlist specific domains, or deny-list private ranges and allow the rest of the internet?
Why the metadata endpoint gets its own control
What "least privilege" means on this path
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The metadata service and how to harden it — AWS: Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata

  • Configuring IMDS options (hop limit, IMDSv2-only) — AWS: Configure the Instance Metadata Service options

  • Pod-level network policy as the isolation primitive — Kubernetes: Network Policies

  • Private address ranges an egress check must deny — RFC 1918 · RFC 3927 (link-local)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The address that must always be blocked? 169.254.169.254 — the link-local metadata endpoint holding instance credentials.
Why is a hostname allowlist insufficient? DNS rebinding. Validate the resolved address, and connect to the address you validated.
What does an IMDS hop limit of 1 achieve? The metadata response can't traverse a container network hop, so a pod can't reach it via the host.
Default posture for an agent's network? Deny all egress, then allow named destinations. Not the reverse.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An agent that can fetch URLs or run tools is an attacker-influenceable HTTP client inside your network, so egress is the control surface. Default-deny outbound, allow a named list, and force every request through a proxy that resolves the host itself, checks the resolved address against private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges, and re-checks on redirects. The proxy runs in its own segment with no IAM role and no route into your VPC, so even a successful injection reaches nothing worth having. And the metadata endpoint is blocked specifically, because it's unauthenticated and holds credentials.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What exactly does a safe egress check look like?

Five steps, in order, and skipping any one of them defeats the rest. Resolve the hostname yourself rather than handing it to an HTTP client. Check every resolved address — a name can resolve to several — against a deny list covering RFC 1918 private ranges, loopback, link-local including the metadata address, unique-local IPv6, and any of your own VPC CIDRs. Connect to the validated address rather than re-resolving by name, which is what closes DNS rebinding. Repeat the whole check on every redirect, because a public URL that 302s to an internal one is the standard bypass. And cap response size and total time, so a fetch can't become a resource-exhaustion vector.

Two additions make it durable. Strip outbound headers the caller didn't intend — an Authorization header leaking onto an arbitrary third-party host is a credential disclosure with no attacker effort. And run the proxy somewhere that can't help even if the check fails: a separate subnet or VPC, no instance role, no peering, no route to internal services. Defence in depth here is cheap, and the check will eventually have a bug.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Allowlist specific domains, or deny-list private ranges and allow the rest of the internet?

An allowlist is the stronger control and is achievable when the agent's job is bounded — a support agent that reads your docs site and your ticketing API needs three domains, and enumerating them makes exfiltration nearly impossible because there's nowhere to send data. The cost is operational: every new integration is a change request, and users experience refusals for legitimate destinations, which pushes people toward broad wildcards that quietly restore the original problem.

Deny-listing private space and allowing the public internet is what a general browsing agent needs to be useful at all. It stops SSRF into your own infrastructure, which is the highest-severity outcome, but it leaves exfiltration open: an injected instruction can encode data into a URL and fetch an attacker's host, and no address check will object because the destination is a perfectly ordinary public IP.

So the choice tracks what the agent handles. Sensitive data plus broad browsing is the combination to refuse — either narrow the destinations or narrow the data. In between, layered controls help: an allowlist for tools that touch sensitive context, deny-list-plus-logging for general browsing, per-agent egress budgets, and DNS-level logging of every destination so exfiltration is at least detectable after the fact. What I wouldn't do is put a general browsing tool and a credentials-bearing tool in the same execution context.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Control Stops SSRF to internals Stops exfiltration Operational cost Where it belongs
Domain allowlist ✅ ✅ mostly high — every integration is a change Agents touching sensitive data
Resolved-IP deny list ✅ ❌ low Any URL-fetching tool, minimum bar
No IAM role on the egress path ✅ removes the prize ❌ low Always
IMDSv2 + hop limit 1 ✅ for metadata specifically ❌ low Always, on every node
Network policy / separate VPC ✅ ❌ medium Sandboxed code execution
DNS + destination logging ❌ detects only ❌ detects only low Always — it's how you find out

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Why the metadata endpoint gets its own control

169.254.169.254 is link-local, unauthenticated at the network layer, and returns credentials for whatever role the instance carries. That combination makes it the highest-value SSRF target in any cloud environment, and it's reachable from any process on the host by default. Two hardening steps are worth applying regardless of your proxy: require IMDSv2, which needs a PUT to obtain a session token and therefore defeats the simple GET-only SSRF shape; and set the hop limit to 1, so the response cannot traverse an extra network hop — which is what stops a container reaching the host's metadata service through the container network. Both are instance-level settings, both are cheap, and neither depends on your application code being correct.

What "least privilege" means on this path

The egress path should hold nothing worth stealing. No instance role, no long-lived credentials in the environment, no peering to internal networks, no DNS view of internal names. Then a bypass of the address check reaches the public internet from an anonymous host — bad, but survivable — rather than reaching your control plane. The rule of thumb: assume the URL check will fail one day, and design so that failure is not a breach.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't rely on the model refusing. Prompt injection is not a solved problem, and "the model wouldn't fetch that" is a hope, not a control. The network layer must hold even when the model is fully cooperative with the attacker.

  • Don't run the fetch in a process that has an IAM role. Removing the credentials removes the prize, and it's a configuration change rather than a code change.

  • Don't allowlist by hostname alone. Validate the resolved address, connect to it directly, and re-check on redirects — otherwise rebinding and redirect chains defeat you.

  • Don't put a browsing tool and a sensitive-data tool in one execution context. Broad egress plus sensitive context is exfiltration waiting for a poisoned page.

  • Don't skip logging because you have a deny list. Address checks stop SSRF and do nothing about exfiltration to public hosts. Destination logs are how you find out it happened.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "We block private IPs, so SSRF is handled."

✅ Reality: It handles reaching your infrastructure and nothing else. Data exfiltration to an attacker-controlled public host passes every address check by design, because the destination is a legitimate public IP. That risk is addressed by allowlisting and by not combining sensitive context with broad egress, not by IP filtering.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought validating the URL before the request was sufficient. Between validation and connection the name can resolve differently, and a redirect can point anywhere — so the control has to be "connect to the address you checked, and re-check every hop", which most HTTP clients will not do unless you make them.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 12-private-vs-public-ip.md and 11-subnets-cidr.md — the ranges a deny list must cover

notes.title: Cost & Data-Path Design for AI Workloads

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Where does the money actually go on an AI data path?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Single-AZ GPU pool for cost, or multi-AZ for availability?
The two calculations worth doing before the design review
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Where data-transfer charges actually apply — AWS: Understanding data transfer charges

  • The per-architecture breakdown — AWS Architecture Blog: Overview of Data Transfer Costs for Common Architectures

  • NAT Gateway and VPC endpoint pricing — Amazon VPC Pricing

  • Why prompt reuse is a compute-cost lever too — vLLM: Automatic Prefix Caching

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which traffic is charged in both directions? Cross-AZ. You pay on the way out and the way in — the surprise on every bill.
What makes model-weight pulls expensive? Tens of GB per replica, through a NAT gateway, on every scale-out and every node replacement.
The single cheapest data-path fix? VPC endpoints for object storage, so weight pulls bypass the NAT gateway entirely.
Which round trip is easiest to overlook? Vector-DB retrieval — small payloads, high frequency, and it's inside your TTFT budget.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

AI workloads move an unusual mix of traffic: tiny, latency-critical vector queries; enormous, bursty model-weight pulls; and a steady stream of token bytes to users. The costs concentrate in three places. Cross-AZ traffic between your gateway and GPU nodes is billed in both directions and adds up because it's on every request. Weight pulls are tens of gigabytes per replica through a NAT gateway unless you use a VPC endpoint. And GPU nodes are scarce and expensive, so scheduling them across AZs for availability quietly buys you a per-request transfer charge.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Where does the money actually go on an AI data path?

Four line items, in rough order of surprise. Cross-AZ transfer: charged in both directions, per gigabyte, on traffic that most architectures generate constantly — gateway to GPU node, GPU node to vector DB, application to cache. It's small per request and enormous in aggregate, and it's invisible until someone reads the bill line rather than the compute line.

NAT gateway processing: charged per gigabyte on top of transfer, and every byte a private-subnet node pulls from the internet or from object storage over a public endpoint goes through it. Model weights are the pathological case — tens of gigabytes per replica, repeated on every scale-out event.

Internet egress: token bytes to users are small, but for a high-volume streaming product they're continuous, and SSE framing adds a modest overhead per token that is worth knowing about even though it rarely dominates.

Inter-node traffic for distributed inference: if a model is sharded across GPUs on different nodes, the activations crossing between them are both a latency and a cost item, which is why multi-GPU serving strongly prefers a single node with fast interconnect.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Single-AZ GPU pool for cost, or multi-AZ for availability?

Single-AZ removes cross-AZ transfer from every request and makes GPU capacity easier to obtain — scarce instance types are allocated per AZ, so concentrating improves your odds of getting them at all. For a workload where the gateway and the GPUs talk constantly, that's a real saving and a real operational benefit.

Multi-AZ is the standard availability posture, and giving it up means an AZ event takes your inference offline entirely. The cost is that every request crossing an AZ boundary is billed both ways, and with an inference gateway in one AZ and replicas spread across three, roughly two-thirds of requests cross.

The design that gets both is zonal alignment rather than a binary choice: run a full stack per AZ — gateway plus GPU replicas — and route within the zone, so cross-AZ traffic happens only on failover. That keeps multi-AZ resilience while making the common path zone-local, and it's the pattern worth naming because it turns an either/or into a routing decision. The residual cost is capacity headroom in each zone, which is real money on GPUs and is the honest trade.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Traffic Volume shape Cost driver The fix
Gateway → GPU node small, constant cross-AZ, both directions Zonal alignment; route within the AZ
Model weight pulls 10s of GB, bursty NAT gateway processing + transfer VPC endpoint to object storage; local node cache; pre-baked images
Vector DB queries small, very frequent cross-AZ + latency inside TTFT Co-locate with the gateway; batch retrievals
Tokens to users small per token, continuous internet egress CDN for static assets only; egress is unavoidable for the stream
Distributed-inference activations large, per token inter-node bandwidth and latency Keep a sharded model on one node with a fast interconnect
TURN-relayed audio (voice) continuous, per call relay bandwidth billed as egress Maximise direct paths; regional TURN placement

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The two calculations worth doing before the design review

Weight-pull cost per scale-out. replicas_added × model_size_GB × ($/GB NAT processing + $/GB transfer). Scaling out twenty replicas of a 40 GB model is 800 GB moved, and if it goes through a NAT gateway that's a charge repeated on every scale event, every node replacement, and every rollout. A VPC endpoint to object storage removes the NAT component entirely, and caching weights on the node's local disk removes most of the repeats — which together turn a recurring line item into a one-off per node.

Cross-AZ cost per request. requests/day × bytes_per_request × 2 × $/GB — the factor of two because cross-AZ is billed in both directions. Per request it's fractions of a cent; at scale it's a line item that surprises people precisely because no single request looks expensive. The point of computing it is not usually to eliminate it but to decide whether zonal alignment is worth the capacity headroom it costs.

And one non-network lever that belongs in the same conversation: prefix caching. Prompt tokens you don't recompute are GPU-seconds you don't buy, and on a workload with a long shared system prompt that dwarfs every transfer charge on this page. Cost design for AI systems that stops at the network has missed the largest term.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't optimise transfer costs before compute costs. GPU time dominates almost every AI bill. Data-path work matters, and it matters second — leading with it signals you haven't seen a real invoice.

  • Don't collapse to a single AZ without saying what you gave up. It removes cross-AZ charges and makes an AZ event a full outage. That's a legitimate trade for some workloads and never a silent one.

  • Don't pull model weights through a NAT gateway. A VPC endpoint costs a small hourly charge and removes per-gigabyte processing on the largest transfers you do.

  • Don't shard a model across nodes to fit it if a bigger single node exists. Inter-node activation traffic is a latency and cost penalty on every token, not just at load time.

  • Don't put a CDN in front of the token stream expecting savings. Egress for token bytes is small and unavoidable; the CDN earns its place on static assets and on connection setup, not on the stream itself.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Traffic inside the VPC is free."

✅ Reality: Same-AZ within a VPC is generally free; cross-AZ is charged, and charged in both directions. A gateway in one AZ talking to replicas in three means most requests are paying twice, and it shows up as a transfer line nobody attributes to the inference service.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated model-weight pulls as a one-time cost at deployment. They repeat on every scale-out, every node replacement and every rollout — so on an autoscaling GPU fleet they're a recurring charge proportional to churn, and the fix (VPC endpoint plus a node-local cache) is configuration rather than architecture.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 172-inference-load-balancing.md — routing decides which traffic crosses a zone boundary

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 177-multi-tenant-isolation.md — attributing this cost per tenant

  • Cross-folder: model serving, batching and GPU utilisation → LLM folder; retrieval latency and caching → RAG folder §12

notes.title: Multi-Tenant Isolation on the Network Path

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
What unit do you rate-limit on, and where do you enforce it?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Shared pool with quotas, or dedicated capacity per tenant?
The arithmetic of local versus global limits
Why the token quota is charged twice
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Distributed quota enforcement at the proxy — Envoy: Global rate limiting

  • Per-instance limits, and why they're not the same thing — Envoy: Local rate limiting

  • 429 and Retry-After semantics (normative) — RFC 6585 · RFC 9110 §10.2.3

  • Shedding rather than queueing under overload — Google SRE Book: Handling Overload

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why is requests-per-second the wrong unit here? Requests differ by orders of magnitude in GPU cost. Limit on tokens or concurrency, not RPS.
Local vs global rate limiting? Local is per proxy instance and approximate; global consults a shared service and is exact but adds a hop.
What must a 429 carry? Retry-After, plus per-tenant limit headers so the client can self-pace instead of hammering.
The isolation that actually stops noisy neighbours? Separate pools or concurrency budgets per tenant class — limits alone don't stop queue contention.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Multi-tenant inference has a noisy-neighbour problem that ordinary APIs don't, because one tenant's request can cost a hundred times another's. So the limit has to be denominated in something that tracks GPU work — tokens per minute, or concurrent requests — rather than requests per second, and it has to be enforced at the gateway where the whole picture is visible. Above that, real isolation needs separate pools or concurrency budgets per tenant class, because a shared queue means a large tenant's long-context requests set everyone's tail latency even while staying inside their quota.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What unit do you rate-limit on, and where do you enforce it?

Not requests per second. A 200-token chat turn and a 20,000-token RAG request both count as one request and differ by two orders of magnitude in GPU work, so an RPS limit either throttles small requests unnecessarily or lets a handful of large ones consume the fleet. The units that track cost are tokens per minute — usually input and output counted separately, since prefill and decode have different cost profiles — and concurrent requests, which bounds how much of the fleet one tenant can occupy at any instant. Most production systems enforce both: tokens for fairness over time, concurrency for protection right now.

Enforcement belongs at the gateway, because that's the only place with a complete view of a tenant across all replicas. Local rate limiting at each proxy instance is cheap and approximate — with N instances, a tenant can exceed the intended limit by up to N times unless you divide it, and dividing it wastes capacity when traffic is uneven. Global rate limiting consults a shared counter service, which is exact and adds a round trip on the request path. The usual compromise is local limits as a fast, generous backstop plus global limits for the real quota.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Shared pool with quotas, or dedicated capacity per tenant?

A shared pool with quotas is far more efficient: GPUs are expensive and idle capacity is waste, so pooling across tenants whose peaks don't coincide is the whole economic argument for a multi-tenant platform. Quotas make it fair on average. What they don't give you is isolation of the tail — a tenant inside their token quota can still fill the queue with long-context requests and lift p99 latency for everyone sharing those replicas, because the queue is shared even when the quota isn't.

Dedicated capacity gives real isolation and costs idle GPUs. It's the right answer for a small number of large customers with contractual latency guarantees, and it's economically indefensible below that scale.

The design that usually wins is tiered pools rather than per-tenant ones: a pool for interactive short-prompt traffic, a pool for long-context and batch, and dedicated pools only for the handful of tenants whose contracts require it. That contains the tail problem — long requests can't starve short ones because they're not in the same queue — without buying idle capacity per customer. Add per-tenant concurrency caps inside each pool, and admission control that sheds with 429 rather than queueing when the pool saturates, because an unbounded queue converts one tenant's burst into everyone's timeout.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Control Stops unfair usage Stops tail contention Cost Where it belongs
RPS limit ❌ (wrong unit) ❌ low Nowhere on an inference path
Tokens-per-minute quota ✅ ❌ low The primary fairness control
Per-tenant concurrency cap ✅ partly low Alongside the token quota
Tiered pools by traffic class — ✅ medium The main isolation mechanism
Dedicated pool per tenant ✅ ✅ high — idle GPUs Contractual guarantees only
Admission control (429) — ✅ under overload low The gateway, always

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic of local versus global limits

With N gateway instances and a tenant quota Q, purely local enforcement lets the tenant reach N × Q if their traffic spreads evenly, so the effective limit depends on your fleet size — which changes with autoscaling. Dividing the quota (Q/N per instance) fixes the ceiling and wastes capacity whenever traffic is uneven, because a tenant hitting one instance is throttled at a fraction of their entitlement while other instances sit unused. Global limiting with a shared counter removes both problems and adds a network round trip to every request plus a dependency that must be highly available and fail open — because a rate limiter that fails closed takes down the platform it was protecting.

Why the token quota is charged twice

Prefill and decode cost differently and are known at different times: input tokens are countable when the request arrives, output tokens only as they're produced. So a workable scheme reserves an estimate on admission (input tokens plus the requested max_tokens) and reconciles against actuals on completion, releasing the difference. Charging only on completion lets a tenant launch unlimited concurrent requests before any of them count; charging only the estimate over-throttles tenants whose responses are short. This is also why the concurrency cap exists — it bounds the exposure between admission and reconciliation.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't limit on requests per second. It's the wrong unit by two orders of magnitude on this workload, and it produces limits that are simultaneously too tight for small requests and too loose for large ones.

  • Don't rely on quotas alone for isolation. A tenant inside quota can still fill a shared queue with long-context requests and lift everyone's p99. Separate pools by traffic class are what actually isolate.

  • Don't queue indefinitely when a pool saturates. Shed with 429 and Retry-After. Queueing converts one tenant's burst into timeouts for everyone and invites a retry storm on top.

  • Don't build a global rate limiter that fails closed. A limiter outage should degrade to local approximate limits, not to a platform outage.

  • Don't give every tenant a dedicated pool. Idle GPUs are the most expensive idle resource you own; reserve dedication for contractual guarantees.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Per-tenant rate limits solve the noisy-neighbour problem."

✅ Reality: They solve fairness of consumption. They don't solve queue contention — a tenant well inside their quota can still occupy replicas with expensive requests and raise the tail for everyone in that pool. Isolation comes from separate pools and concurrency caps; quotas are the accounting layer on top.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I enforced limits per gateway instance and assumed the total was roughly right. With an autoscaling fleet the effective limit is the per-instance limit times however many instances exist that minute — so the quota silently loosened under load, exactly when it was needed. Global counters with local backstops is the shape that survives autoscaling.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 172-inference-load-balancing.md — the pools and routing this enforces on top of
